World.title: The Costa Rica I Remember From the 1990s
World.content:
Lately I have seen an abundance of AI-generated clips portraying happy scenes of how life was back in the day. One shows Christmas 1985, all a pictorial representation of a song such as White Christmas, with treetops glistening and children listening to hear sleigh bells in the snow. Inside the house, a roaring fireplace, a decorated tree with presents piled beneath, and mom in the kitchen making cookies.

Of course, the reality is different. My memory of that same Christmas season is working overtime, my girlfriend moving out and a close friend dying. It is easy to look back wistfully, and unrealistically, through eyes that wish those days had never ended.

I sometimes find myself experiencing the same romantic look back when I think of my first years in Costa Rica. The year 1990 was a time of optimism. The Berlin Wall had fallen, the Soviet Union had collapsed, dictators in Central America were replaced by legally elected leaders, and here in Costa Rica, Oscar Arias was honored with a Nobel Prize a couple years before for authoring the Central American Peace Plan.

Even the hit songs reflected this. Right Here, Right Now by Jesus Jones and Winds of Change by the Scorpions celebrated this changing world. Of course, I can name things that I do not miss about those days: unpaved, potholed roads, one-lane bridges everywhere, too many people throwing personal trash out the window of a moving vehicle, no decent phone service outside the San José metro area, and the inability to find good peanut butter, among other things.

Progress was inevitable, and I welcome those changes that brought us into the modern day. Beyond this, there are things I still miss about the Costa Rica I knew. Here are a few.

Cash was king

Debit cards were still a few years away, SINPE a couple decades away. Instead of plastic cards and numbers on a screen, you carried something tangible, real bills with big numbers on them that were accepted everywhere.

A monthly trip to the bank to withdraw dollars, which I then exchanged with a trusted money changer who had his own office on Avenida Segunda and paid a slightly better rate than the bank, and I was set for the next few weeks.

Speaking of the exchange rate

Even then Costa Rica was not a cheap destination. But the exchange rate was reasonable, and those in charge had implemented an automatic gradual devaluation that slowly but continually yielded more colones for each dollar.

The exchange rate shot from 100 to the dollar in 1990 to 500 to the dollar in 2006, and has since been a series of peaks and valleys, though what we are experiencing now seems more like a plunge into the abyss than a valley.

Less taxation

The 13% VAT was a long way away. There was a standard 10% sales tax that was factored into the price of most items. It was applied additionally on bigger-ticket items like cars, building materials and appliances. I ran a home-based baking business for years that was strictly cash and carry. The stores I worked with all accepted handwritten receipts and paid me in cash.

Then came facturas timbradas, registering your business with the government, taxable income, and no more flying under the radar, except when doing business with others also flying under the radar.

No influencers

The damnable word had not yet been coined. The pre-influencer era spared us from those who use our many spectacular sites as backdrops for their selfies, and regale us from the perspective of a self-styled expert who has been in Costa Rica two years and has a 200-word Spanish vocabulary.

Obesity was rare

One of my first observations on arrival was that the whole country looked physically fit. The first village I lived in was in the Zona Sur. The two noticeably overweight men in town were also the two most prosperous, ranchers with large herds of cattle and other side investments in the area. They lived a comparative high life, and it showed.

Today there are tens of thousands as obese as the two ranchers, but it is mostly a result of poor diets laden with sugar, manteca and excess starches. More Ticos are prosperous, so maybe there is a correlation to be made between prosperity and eating, drinking and being merry to excess.

Murder was not an everyday occurrence

Cocaine and cartel-related violence was rare. There were sensational cases, such as the psicópata, a never-apprehended serial killer who numbered 19 victims in the late 1980s and early 1990s, many of them couples in secluded areas of the Central Valley.

But the numbers do not lie. In 1991 there were 132 murders, or 4.1 per 100,000 people. In 2025 there were 873 murders, 2.4 per day and 17 per 100,000.

There was more space for everyone

The population went from 3 million and change to 5 million and change. The number of vehicles on the road, and this number is staggering, went from 300,000 in 1990 to nearly 2 million in 2025, an almost sevenfold increase. And, of course, more developments, more hotels, more pieces of nature cleared and replaced by a concrete and steel structure.

I can only imagine how the AI of 2060 will look back upon present-day Costa Rica. Will today’s Costa Rica look quaint? Will people look back wistfully at bygone days, wishing they could recapture those moments?

Hell if I know. If I am still alive then I will be a centenarian and cannot imagine being that old and thinking about anything more than getting through the day.

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Why “Diablo” Got Only Three Months in Costa Rica Custody
World.content:
A Costa Rican court has ordered three months and 22 days of preventive detention for a man surnamed Arias, known by the alias “Diablo,” in a resolution issued yesterday. The term runs from the date of his detention on July 24 to November 16, 2026. In the same resolution, the court imposed five months and 26 days on a co-defendant surnamed Pérez, alias “Tan,” a period that expires on December 27, 2026.

The numbers were read by much of us as an anticlimax, and the criticism reached the top of the executive branch. Before the Public Ministry issued its explanation, President Laura Fernández said publicly that a three-month term would be the greatest embarrassment the judiciary could produce. Legislator Kattia Calvo separately questioned the result. Neither reaction accounted for what the Public Ministry set out hours later, which is that the terms are a statutory ceiling rather than a measure of how seriously the court treats the case.

Under ordinary criminal jurisdiction in Costa Rica, preventive detention in a single case is capped at 18 months. Both men had already spent time in preventive custody during earlier stages of this same file. What the Tribunal Penal del II Circuito Judicial de Limón granted yesterday was not a fresh term but the unused remainder of that 18-month allowance — three months and 22 days left for Arias, five months and 26 days for Pérez.

The Fiscalía Adjunta contra la Delincuencia Organizada asked for exactly those figures because they were the only ones available to it. The hearing began at 1:30 p.m. and was held in private at the Tribunales del I Circuito Judicial de San José, moved there from Pococí for security reasons.

November 16 is therefore a procedural checkpoint rather than a release date. The Public Ministry has said the expiry of the term does not mean either man automatically walks free, and that it will seek an extension before the Tribunal Penal de Apelación de Sentencia, the body that decides preventive detention once the ordinary 18-month limit has been exhausted.

The court also declared the case one of organized crime, applying article 10, subsection 1 of Law 9481, which created Costa Rica’s specialized organized crime jurisdiction. That declaration moves the file out of ordinary jurisdiction, and the Public Ministry has said it will ask the specialized tribunal to take over several of the causes against both men. If that request is granted, the maximum preventive detention terms available in the case can double.

The file on which yesterday’s order was issued concerns two homicides and one attempted homicide, allegedly committed as contract killings, along with a charge of criminal association. The events under investigation date to Pococí in 2015. Neither man has been tried, and both remain presumed innocent.

If you don’t know by now, both were detained during an operation in Sarapiquí that the Organismo de Investigación Judicial named Operation Némesis. Agents were met with gunfire on entering the property, and the exchange lasted roughly an hour. Five OIJ officers were wounded, one seriously enough to be flown to San José by helicopter.

A third man, surnamed Ríos Oconitrillo and known as “Coco Guácimo,” was killed by after firing on agents. Investigators later reported recovering assault rifles, ammunition and drones from the scene, and estimated that some 2,500 rounds were fired. Arias and Pérez are being held in maximum-security cells at La Reforma.

The scale of the case is what has kept it at the center of national attention. OIJ interim director Michael Soto told a press conference at the Supreme Court that the three criminal structures linked to Arias, Pérez and Ríos Oconitrillo are connected to approximately 360 homicides — around 200 attributed to the first group, 100 to the second and 60 to the third.

Soto was explicit that the figure attaches to the structures rather than to the three men individually, and described it as conservative. He said the organizations controlled drug distribution, cigarette and liquor smuggling and score-settling across Pococí, Sarapiquí, the Northern Zone, Cañas, Liberia, Santa Cruz, Turrialba, Quepos, Parrita, Garabito, Osa, Guácimo, Batán, Valle La Estrella and Nicoya.

Soto also warned that removing the leadership of three structures at once could produce violence rather than calm, as sellers inside and outside those groups move to take territory. The precedent he pointed to is the 2012 capture of a man surnamed Zamora Solórzano, alias “El Indio,” which set off a fight over drug-selling zones in southern San José that left more than 110 people dead by 2015. Zamora was sentenced to 70 years in prison in 2015.

Arias’s defense attorney, Cristian Rodríguez, told reporters that his client’s release had been effectively impossible given the years spent as a fugitive, the gravity of the alleged offenses and the new accusations arising from the July 24 operation. Rodríguez has filed a challenge before the tribunal against security measures imposed on his client by the Ministry of Justice, and has said he may take the matter to the Constitutional Chamber.

What happens on November 16 now depends on two decisions that have not yet been made — whether the appeals tribunal grants the extension the Public Ministry has said it will request, and whether the specialized organized crime tribunal assumes the file. Until then, the date on the resolution marks the limit of what one court was permitted to order, not the length of time anyone expects these men to spend in custody.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Widen Extradition of Its Own Citizens
World.content:
President Laura Fernández asked lawmakers on Monday to widen the narrow list of crimes for which Costa Rica may hand its own citizens over to foreign courts, proposing a constitutional amendment that would add money laundering, human trafficking, arms trafficking, contract killing and cybercrime to the two grounds that exist today.

The president arrived at the Legislative Assembly mid-morning accompanied by her cabinet, police directors and members of the unit the government calls Fuerza Élite, and delivered a second package of six security bills. The extradition proposal was the centerpiece of her presentation but was not among the files formally handed over, because legislative procedure does not allow constitutional reforms to be processed during extraordinary sessions. The government said it will file that text on Monday, August 3.

Costa Rica has permitted the extradition of its nationals only since 2025, and only for international drug trafficking and terrorism. Fernández wants to add seven further categories: money laundering; human trafficking and migrant smuggling; illegal arms trafficking; trafficking in organs, tissues and human stem cells; contract killing and homicides linked to organized criminal structures; participation in transnational criminal organizations; and cybercrime, cyberterrorism and cyberfraud that compromise national security or the critical infrastructure of the Costa Rican state.

Fernández framed the proposal as a move against criminal structures rather than a general loosening of protections for citizens, telling lawmakers that Costa Rican nationality is a right and a source of pride for millions of honest citizens and <cite index=”1-1″>not a shield for members of transnational criminal organizations.

She said the mechanism would remain exceptional and would require a final ruling from Costa Rican courts in every case, describing it as not an automatic or generalized extradition of nationals. The proposal also preserves the dual criminality requirement, meaning the conduct must be a crime both in Costa Rica and in the country requesting the person.

The prohibition Fernández is seeking to narrow further dates to the aftermath of the 1948 civil war, when the drafters of the current constitution barred the forced removal of citizens from national territory. That ban held for more than seven decades. The Legislative Assembly approved the amendment to Article 32 unanimously in its final debate on May 15, 2025, and the reform was promulgated as Law 10730 and published on May 28 of that year. A companion reform harmonizing the 1971 Extradition Law with the new constitutional text cleared Congress the following November.

On March 20 of this year, former Supreme Court magistrate and former security minister Celso Gamboa Sánchez and Edwin Danney López Vega were handed to United States agents at the San Jose Airport and flown to Texas aboard a DEA aircraft, the first extraditions of Costa Rican nationals in our history.

Both face cocaine conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of Texas. The appeals court that authorized the transfer required written assurances from Washington that neither man would face life imprisonment or a sentence longer than 50 years, the ceiling permitted under Costa Rican law, and that time served in pretrial detention here would be credited against any sentence.

That same ruling exposed a question the courts have not settled. Judges accepted a defense argument on non-retroactivity in the case of a third man, Álvarez Alfaro, declining to apply the 2025 reform to conduct predating it. Whether nationals can be extradited for acts committed before May 2025 remains contested, and any expansion of the grounds would inherit the same dispute.

Constitutional amendments move slowly in Costa Rica by design. The text must win a two-thirds majority in three debates, then be taken up again and approved in three more debates after the Assembly’s annual turnover, meaning no reform filed in August could take effect before the second half of the current legislative period at the earliest.

The five bills Fernández did file on Monday address the ordinary criminal system. One would replace the preliminary hearing in the Criminal Procedure Code with a single pre-trial hearing before the same court that will hear the case, which the president said would cut duplicated steps that delay resolutions. Another would require electronic ankle monitoring for anyone granted an alternative to prison after a final sentence, replacing arrangements such as signing in every fifteen days.

A third would classify illegal mining as organized crime and raise penalties for extraction, processing, financing, transport or storage to between six and ten years, with confiscation of machinery and registry freezes on linked properties. A fourth would allow parents jailed over unpaid child support to serve under electronic monitoring instead, on the reasoning that a father in prison cannot earn the money he owes.

The fifth restores older police rank titles and requires a university degree and fifteen years of service for senior command posts. A planned reform of the Dirección de Inteligencia y Seguridad Nacional was pulled from the package and deferred to a third round of bills.

The government has now sent twelve security bills to Congress since mid-June. Homicides, meanwhile, are running below last year’s pace. The Judicial Investigation Agency counted 401 killings through July 6, fifty-two fewer than the same point in 2025, with settling of scores recorded as the leading motive and San José, Limón and Puntarenas the most affected provinces.

World.title: Rare Costa Rica Video Shows Sunbittern Defending Its Ground
World.content:
Today we meet the sunbittern, a unique bird that’s nearly impossible to see until it screams its presence at you. And the remiges? Don’t get me started on the remiges.

The sunbittern (Eurypyga helias) is known as the garza del sol in Spanish which translates to ‘sun heron.’ While the English and Spanish names are similar, they’re both a bit misleading as this bird is not actually related to bitterns nor herons. These birds are the sole member of their taxonomic family. Oddly enough, its closest relative seems to be the kagu which is a wild-looking bird that lives on the opposite side of the planet in New Caledonia.

A succinct physical description of a sunbittern is that it looks like a small heron. It’s a waterbird with longish yellow legs, a long, thin neck, and a straight, pointy beak, but this bird is really two birds packed into one. The calm sunbittern is nearly impossible to see. Its plumage is black and brown with specks of white, allowing it to blend in perfectly with the rocky edge of a stream or the fallen leaves of a forest.

A fired-up sunbittern is a different animal. Whether in the presence of the opposite sex, which requires some wooing, or the presence of a threat, which requires some scaring off, the sunbittern quickly fans its tail and extends its wings vertically transforming it from impossible to see to impossible to miss.

The extension of its wings displays its remiges, the wing-feathers used for flight, which have a beautiful sunburst pattern that resembles two large eyes. During courtship, these beautiful wings exhibit to a potential mate the fitness of the individual. When a sunbittern feels threatened, it displays its wings and charges at the threat, making it appear as though something with two big eyes is coming in hot.

This beautiful bird can be found patrolling quick flowing streams or sometimes swampier environments in forested areas. They eat a diet consistent with the normal waterbird menu, amphibians, crayfish, insects, and small fish. When it comes to nesting behavior, not too much is known because only a few nests have been located in the wild. Generally, the nests are a messy glob of leaves, stems, and sticks, placed a few meters up a tree that sits along a stream where they lay a pair of speckled eggs.

I’ve never actually seen a sunbittern with my two brown eyes, but I have recorded them with my camera traps. I first recorded one a few years ago on a farm in Pérez Zeledón. I recorded a handful of videos of an individual along a fast-flowing forest stream. It even displayed its wings in one of the videos, but it didn’t quite scratch the itch of recording a really good sunbittern video because it was too far away.

After that, I decided to wait until I recorded a really nice video of one displaying its wings directly in front of the camera before I wrote a Tico Times article about the species. Well, you’re reading the article so you can guess what happened recently. A few months ago, I got a video of one aggressively displaying its wings at a brown basilisk and then chasing it off.

It was an excellent video, but it happened in the early morning when there wasn’t a lot of light, so the video was in black and white, not really showing off the wing display in the way I wanted. A few days ago, I recorded the video I was waiting for on a forest trail just above a stream.

A male great curassow walked out of the forest directly in front of the camera causing a sunbittern farther up the trail to display its wings and charge forward. The curassow took off, leaving the sunbittern to display its wings directly at the lens of the camera. The wait was over and the article could be written. Take a look at the long anticipated video below.

World.title: Rincón de la Vieja volcano raised to caution level after 38 eruptions
World.content:
If you have a Rincón de la Vieja hike or a hot springs day trip on your calendar, the volcano’s official activity level went up last week — and the change is worth not only knowing about but understanding before you drive out there.

The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVISCORI) moved Rincón de la Vieja from warning to caution on 24 July, the third rung on a four-step scale. Since 2 July the observatory has counted 38 phreatic eruptions at the crater. Three of them sent lahars down the northern flank. The strongest, on 20 July, was the most energetic eruption the volcano has produced all year.

Volcanologist Geoffroy Avard said the decision rested on more than the eruption count. Seismic activity has picked up. The shape of the volcano itself is changing measurably and to get technical, the Sulphur dioxide output is up. Put together, those three signals point the same direction, and the observatory said further eruptions of equal or greater intensity are possible. In a nutshell, this is not a report that something happened but a report that something is more likely to happen again.

What caution actually means

Costa Rica’s volcano scale runs from one to four. Level one is calm. Level two, warning, is where Rincón de la Vieja has spent most of the last several years — small eruptions, gas, hot springs bubbling harder than usual, mild swelling of the summit. Ash falls lightly if it falls at all.

Level three, caution, is a step up in what the volcano is capable of on short notice, not a declaration that it is erupting now. It means bigger explosions are on the table, rocks can be thrown further from the crater, ash can travel, and lahars are an expected consequence rather than a surprise. Level four is reserved for a major eruption in progress.

Nothing about level three closes the area, cancels flights or triggers evacuations. What it does is shrink the margin for error close to the crater, which is exactly where the hardest hiking in the park goes.

Why the rivers turn grey

Those downhill from the volcano reported the Azul and Pénjamo rivers running a milky grey earlier this month after eruptive episodes. That color is the most reliable early warning system in the area, and it is worth knowing what it signals.

Rincón de la Vieja has an acidic lake sitting inside its active crater. A phreatic eruption happens when groundwater or lake water hits something hot enough to flash it to steam, and the pressure blows out through the top. There is no lava involved. What comes out is steam, gas, rock and a great deal of water and sediment.

That water and sediment goes somewhere. The crater’s northern rim is the lowest, so the flow spills that way and races downhill as a lahar — essentially a fast-moving slurry of water, ash, mud and rock with the consistency of wet concrete. It picks up more material from the riverbed as it goes. By the time it reaches the lowland farming communities on the Upala side, the river is grey, smells of sulphur and is running higher than it was an hour earlier.

Rain makes this worse rather than better, which is important to know in late July. Heavy rain at the summit mobilizes loose volcanic material that is already sitting on the slopes, so a lahar can come down without a fresh eruption to announce it.

The historical record shows what these flows can do. In November 1995 a lahar took out the bridge over the Pénjamo entirely. In 2019 the same river rose more than four metres (13 feet) in minutes and widened by six metres (20 feet) on each bank. Dead fish have turned up in the Río Niño, 15 kilometres (nine miles) from the crater, after past events.

If you are near one of these rivers and the water changes color, rises or starts to smell of sulphur, get away from the channel and onto higher ground. Do not wait to see how big it gets. That is the whole safety rule, and it works because lahars travel much faster than people can outrun them along a riverbed.

What is open in the park

Rincón de la Vieja National Park covers 14,300 hectares (35,300 acres) and is the busiest protected area in the Guanacaste Conservation Area. It sits about 23 kilometres (14 miles) from Liberia, which is why it shows up on so many itineraries. Visitation splits between two sectors, Las Pailas and Santa María.

The Active Crater trail — eight kilometres one way, 16 kilometres (10 miles) round trip, climbing roughly 1,000 metres (3,300 feet) — has been closed for years. Volcanic activity and unsafe crater gases keep it shut, and last week’s level change does nothing to reopen it. Anyone selling you a summit hike is selling you something the park is not permitting.

The Las Pailas loop is the main draw and the reason most visitors come. It runs three kilometres (1.9 miles) on a circuit past fumaroles, boiling mud pots and steam vents that sit between 78 and 106 degrees Celsius (172 to 223 degrees Fahrenheit). It is well marked and partly paved. The waterfall trails to La Cangreja, five kilometres (3.1 miles) out, and Catarata Escondida, 4.3 kilometres (2.7 miles), are longer and harder.

Confirm the day before you go. Area and trail closures at this park have historically arrived with no notice, sometimes on the morning of, and travelers have turned up at the gate to be told a trail shut days earlier. Park staff at the entrance know the current status. A tour operator’s website from last season does not.

All tickets must be bought in advance through the park service’s online reservation system. There is no cash or card payment at the gate.

What closes first if the level rises

The pattern here in Costa Rica is consistent, and it works outward from the crater. Summit and crater-adjacent trails go first — those are already shut here. Next come the longer backcountry trails that put hikers hours from an exit, which is where the waterfall routes sit. Then the visited sectors themselves close, sometimes one at a time, sometimes both.

Hot springs resorts and private reserves on the volcano’s flanks operate independently of the park and make their own calls, so a park closure does not automatically mean your hot springs booking is cancelled, or the reverse. Full closures of an entire area have happened repeatedly at active volcanoes and have lasted anywhere from a day to several weeks. Build that possibility into a tight Guanacaste itinerary rather than assuming a single fixed day at the park will hold.

Poás is active too

Rincón de la Vieja is not the only volcano the observatory is watching. Poás, far more accessible from the Central Valley and San José, is producing low-intensity eruptions of its own. Poás has its own history of abrupt closures over gas emissions and ashfall, including multi-week shutdowns. If you are choosing between the two on a short trip, check both before committing.

Where to check

The observatory monitors Rincón de la Vieja continuously through seismic stations, gas-measuring equipment, cameras and field observation, and publishes changes as they happen. Level changes in either direction are announced rather than quietly applied — the volcano was moved down from caution to warning in a previous cycle, and it could go either way again.

The behavior on display now is not new for this mountain. Rincón de la Vieja has run through active phases and quiet ones since 2011, with stretches of daily small eruptions followed by months of little. What the level change records is that the current stretch is more energetic than the last one, and that the instruments suggest it has further to run.

World.title: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament
World.content:
Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars returned home with championship honors after delivering an impressive performance at the XII Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament in Cancún, Quintana Roo, Mexico.

They competed with both its U15 and U17 teams from July 23 to 26, facing strong competition from teams across the region.

Both Gonz Auto Stars teams showcased determination, discipline and teamwork throughout the tournament, battling hard in every game and representing Belize with pride. Their performances reflected the commitment and fighting spirit that have become hallmarks of the Gonz Auto Stars basketball program.

The biggest achievement came from the U17 team, which captured first place to bring the championship title home to Belize. The victory was celebrated as a testament to the players’ hard work, dedication and belief in one another.

The team credited coaches Gabriel Taylor, Ronell Gonzalez Sr., Cordel Gonzalez Jr. and Cordel Gonzalez Sr. for their leadership, preparation and support throughout the tournament.

Gonz Auto Stars also expressed gratitude to its sponsors and everyone who supported the team’s BBQ fundraiser, which helped make the international trip possible.

World.title: Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone
World.content:
Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Lords Bank resident accused of sexually assaulting a 10-year-old girl was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after the Belize City Magistrate’s Court denied his application for bail following detailed submissions from both the prosecution and defense.

Manuel De Jesus Flores, a local mason, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #5 to face two counts of sexual assault. The charges allege that on July 18, 2026, Flores intentionally and unlawfully touched the female minor—who is 10 years and 5 months old—in a sexual manner without her consent.

The allegations stem from an incident occurring around 12:30 a.m. while the child’s mother was briefly away at a neighboring home. According to court details, the child reported that an elderly man standing at a construction site two lots over motioned for her to come to him. When she refused and went inside, he later entered her yard, asked for a hug, and grabbed her left hand when she attempted to walk away. The assailant then lifted her hips, pressed his erection against her body, touched her inappropriately, and squeezed her breast. Before releasing her, he handed her a $1 coin and a $2 bill, telling her not to tell anyone. The victim threw the money back at him, ran down the street carrying her younger cousin, and met her mother on the road to report what had occurred.

During court proceedings, defense attorney Sharon Pitts-Robateau made extensive submissions advocating for her client’s release, seeking bail even after the sitting Magistrate initially indicated a denial due to the grave nature of the offense. Attorney Pitts highlighted that Flores is gainfully employed as a mason and emphasized the fundamental presumption of innocence, pointing out that the charges are strictly allegations at this stage. She argued that the essential legal purpose of bail is to ensure a defendant returns to court, a goal that could be achieved by setting strict bail conditions rather than remanding him.

Police Prosecutor Sgt. Ayala vigorously countered the application, urging the Senior Magistrate to consider several key factors against granting release. Sgt. Ayala cited the very young age of the victim, the high prevalence and seriousness of sexual assault offenses, and the likelihood that Flores might reoffend given the early morning hour of the alleged incident. The prosecution further argued that releasing the accused would present a significant risk of interference with the young victim or the ongoing police investigation.

After considering the arguments from both sides, the Senior Magistrate sustained the prosecution’s objections and refused bail. Flores was remanded in custody to the Belize Central Prison until his next scheduled court appearance on September 17, 2026.

World.title: Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry
World.content:
Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry

By Zoila Palma: The Central Bank of Belize (the Central Bank), the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), and the Financial Services Commission (FSC) have signed governance agreements establishing the framework for the shared use of the Sanctions Registry System (SRS).

A joint statement explained that SRS is a secure supervisory platform developed by the Central Bank, and designed to support the management of sanctions-related information and strengthen Belize’s framework for combatting money laundering, terrorist financing, and other forms of financial crime. By improving information management, data retrieval, and analytical capability, the system enables a more efficient, consistent, and risk-based approach to supervision.

“The governance agreements provide the legal and operational framework for participating authorities to access and use the SRS in support of their respective statutory responsibilities. While each institution will utilise the system independently within its own supervisory environment, the shared platform promotes greater consistency in regulatory information management and enhances opportunities for collaboration where appropriate,” it added.

The initiative reflects the continued commitment of the Central Bank, the FIU, and the FSC to strengthening inter-agency cooperation through the effective use of technological innovation, improved information sharing, and modern supervisory practices.

The Central Bank, FIU, and FSC said that they remain committed to working collaboratively to strengthen Belize’s regulatory framework, enhance supervisory effectiveness, and promote a safe, sound and resilient financial system.

World.title: International News: PAHO, AIDS Healthcare Foundation partner to expand early HIV diagnosis in Latin America and Caribbean
World.content:
International News: PAHO, AIDS Healthcare Foundation partner to expand early HIV diagnosis in Latin America and Caribbean

By Zoila Palma: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and the AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) are partnering to expand early HIV diagnosis across Latin America and the Caribbean, with the goal of improving access to testing, connecting people to care sooner and reducing preventable AIDS-related deaths.

Despite progress in the regional HIV response, late diagnosis remains a major challenge. PAHO estimates that in 2025, about 34% of new HIV diagnoses in the region were made at an advanced stage of infection, while approximately 32,000 people died from AIDS-related causes. The partnership will focus on expanding testing services and strengthening the link between diagnosis and timely treatment.

The initiative was announced during a PAHO satellite session at the International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026) in Rio de Janeiro, where government representatives, community organizations and international partners discussed barriers to timely HIV diagnosis and treatment. PAHO officials said that although effective testing and treatment options are available, thousands of people continue to be diagnosed only after the disease has progressed.

Through the collaboration, PAHO and AHF will support expanded access to HIV testing, including self-testing and community-based services, while promoting stronger links to care and improved retention in treatment.

In 2025, an estimated 2.1 million people living with HIV in Latin America and the Caribbean were receiving antiretroviral therapy, representing 72% treatment coverage, while about 900,000 people remained without treatment.

The organizations will work with national health authorities, community groups and other partners to adapt strategies to the needs of individual countries.

World.title: International News: Thousands of migrant children’s sponsors arrested after information shared with ICE
World.content:
International News: Thousands of migrant children’s sponsors arrested after information shared with ICE

By Zoila Palma: Thousands of migrant children and their sponsors have been caught up in U.S. immigration enforcement after the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) shared information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to internal government data reviewed by Reuters.

More than 12,000 people have reportedly been arrested following tips from ORR during President Donald Trump’s second term.

The ORR, established in 1980 to assist refugees, also oversees unaccompanied migrant children who arrive at the U.S.-Mexico border. Under longstanding policy, the agency’s work was largely separated from immigration enforcement, allowing children to be released to parents or relatives without fear that sponsors would be targeted for immigration violations.

That approach has shifted significantly under the Trump administration. Since January 2025, ORR has reportedly shared more than 460,000 leads with ICE involving unaccompanied children, their sponsors and other household members.

The Department of Homeland Security said the information has been used to identify potential investigative leads involving children placed with sponsors who may have criminal records or were considered unvetted.

The policy change has raised concerns among immigration advocates and former government officials, who say the sharing of information has undermined trust in the child welfare system.

World.title: Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee and partners discuss Belize Environmental Geoportal
World.content:
Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee and partners discuss Belize Environmental Geoportal

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Environmental Statistics Advisory Committee (ESAC) convened its third meeting, bringing together representatives from key government agencies and partner organizations to advance the production, management, and dissemination of environmental statistics in Belize.

Discussions included updating the Belize Environmental Geoportal.

Participants joined an interactive session with consultant Yvette Alonzo, who is leading the validation and updating of the Belize Environmental Geoportal.

Committee members reviewed existing datasets, identified priority data gaps, and provided recommendations to further enhance the Geoportal as a centralized platform for environmental information.

The Department of the Environment explained that the Belize Environmental Geoportal plays a vital role in supporting evidence-based decision-making, national and international environmental reporting, and public access to reliable environmental data. Through continued collaboration, ESAC remains committed to strengthening Belize’s environmental information systems and ensuring that accurate, up-to-date environmental data is available to support sustainable development and informed policymaking.

World.title: Belize Police Department hosts 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program
World.content:
Belize Police Department hosts 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department (BPD) is hosting the 27th Annual Cadet Corps Summer Program.

The program features a vibrant fusion of education, culture, and spirited competition, as 279 cadets from across Belize gathered at Ecumenical High School.

Sessions include personal and community development, featuring rotational lectures delivered by Community Policing Officers on essential topics including Anger Management, Knowing Your Community, and Effective Communication. Building on this foundation of knowledge, the cadets then engaged with interactive educational booth displays presented by the National Drug Abuse Control Council (NDACC), the Ministry of Rural Transformation, and the Department of Youth Services.

In addition, cadets enjoyed a lively practical dance session led by the Hanigi Cultural Dance Group, allowing the young participants to celebrate Belize’s rich heritage through movement.

“The spirit of camaraderie carried into the afternoon as the cadets transitioned to the auditorium for a high-energy volleyball competition.

Displaying exceptional athleticism and teamwork, the Eastern Region emerged victorious, clinching the title after winning two of three sets, with the Northern Region securing a strong second place, followed by the South in third, and the West rounding out the top four,” the BPD said.

The cadets also participated in cultural presentations from the various precincts, showcasing the diverse talents within the corps and solidifying another successful day of growth and unity at the annual summer program.

World.title: Belize Bank invests in Belize’s future, awards scholarships to 16 Students!
World.content:
Belize Bank invests in Belize’s future, awards scholarships to 16 Students!

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Bank Limited has awarded scholarships to 16 students from across the country as part of its 14th Annual Scholarship Award Ceremony.

The scholarships are awarded based on academic excellence and financial need and are aimed at supporting students in pursuing their educational goals.

The Belize Bank said that since the scholarship program began, it has invested in the education of 230 Belizean youths, including 140 high school students and 90 sixth form scholars. The 2026 recipients join the program’s growing network of young Belizeans receiving financial support and mentorship.

The ceremony featured the participation of Minister of State in the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, Ramon Cervantes, who delivered the keynote address and highlighted the importance of accessible education.

Belize Bank Chairman and CEO Filippo Alario also addressed the students, emphasizing the importance of family support and the bank’s mentorship program, which connects scholars with bank managers for professional guidance.

The scholarship program provides full tuition and school fees, school supplies and mentorship.

High school recipients receive four years of support, including an annual $300 book grant, while 6th form scholars receive two years of support valued at $3,000 annually for tuition and school fees, along with professional mentorship and career guidance.

The 2026 scholarship recipients include 6th form scholars Aaron Bradley, Itzany Montes, Markell Pott, Aliza Doniz, Jaylen Hendy and Ezequiel Blanco. High school scholars are Zion Santos, Zairen Carrillo, Kryselle Arjona, Nimrod Fitzgibbon, Juliana Belisle, Khaleesi Neal, Yendi Flowers, Franklin Diaz, Jorge Mancia and Shaquana Ciego.

World.title: Conflict shift
World.content:
Superintendent Mark Harris, commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division, speaks about the division’s changing crime landscape during an episode of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Force4Good podcast. x

THE St Andrew Central Police Division, which is the commercial heartbeat of the Corporate Area, where thousands of Jamaicans live and work daily, is confronting a changing crime landscape, with police saying interpersonal and domestic conflicts have become a greater concern than organised gang violence.

Commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division Superintendent Mark Harris said the division has largely brought organised gang activity under control, but is now grappling with murders arising from personal disputes, many of which occur without warning and in communities not traditionally associated with violent crime. He said this shift has presented a more complex policing challenge because, unlike gang conflicts, interpersonal disputes are far less predictable.

Speaking on the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Force4Good podcast, Harris said the division recorded the largest reduction in murders across the Jamaica Constabulary Force last year and even went an entire month without a murder this February. However, he noted that while gang-related killings have declined significantly, police are increasingly being challenged by crimes rooted in personal and domestic disputes.

“Last year, I had gang issues, [but] this year, we don’t have a gang issue, we have criminals committing crimes, but it’s not associated with gangs, like 2024 and part of 2025, and believe it or not, gang conflict is easier to police than the interpersonal and the domestic issues,” he noted.

The St Andrew Central Police Division encompasses some of Jamaica’s busiest commercial, educational and transport hubs, including Half-Way-Tree, New Kingston, Cross Roads and Papine. It is also responsible for policing major national events, entertainment activities and sporting fixtures that are often held at the National Stadium, making it one of the JCF’s most demanding divisions.

The division also includes communities such as August Town and Nannyville, both of which have experienced persistent gang activity and periodic security operations over the years. August Town was placed under a Zone of Special Operations in 2020 following years of deadly gang violence, while Nannyville has repeatedly featured in anti-gang and anti-gun operations as police sought to dismantle organised criminal networks operating across Kingston and St Andrew.

Despite that history, Harris said the division’s greatest challenge is no longer organised gangs but the rise in deadly interpersonal conflicts.

“We know where the gangs are and where they operate and who they’re in conflict with, and we put police right there…but for the interpersonal things, even in Jack’s Hill we have murders [and] that is not normally a place where we have murders… and these are interpersonal, rather than gang conflict,” he explained.

He said the division is relying not only on intelligence-led operations but also stronger community partnerships to prevent personal disputes from escalating into violence.

“We go out there and do the hard policing, we still have our community engagement. We had to do those meetings at the Transport Centre to speak to students and parents and stakeholders,” Harris noted.

Meanwhile, Area Four Commander Assistant Commissioner of Police Michael Phipps said St Andrew Central remains critical to crime management across Kingston and St Andrew because of its concentration of commercial activity, major institutions and daily commuter traffic.

He noted that the division has also experienced a significant number of fatal attacks involving weapons other than firearms, reflecting the growing challenge posed by interpersonal violence.

“I can tell you here and now that St Andrew Central has had a very high number of murders resulting from the use of knives and other blunt-force trauma injuries that have resulted in death. So we see St Andrew Central as one of the most important divisions if we are to maintain control of crime across Area Four,” Phipps said.

World.title: Upper St Andrew residents ready to protest
World.content:
The residents of Kingston 8 claim that a lot of the problems they face stem from an increase in large real estate projects in the area, as when projects are being executed, roads are dug up and not repaired properly. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

SOME residents of upper St Andrew have threatened to take up placards to protest poor road infrastructure and unrestricted real estate developments, as they say they are tired of their cries falling on deaf ears.

The Jamaica Observer was taken on a tour of Waterworks Road and adjoining thoroughfares in Kingston 8, starting from the Manor Park area, where various roadways that were recently patched have already started disintegrating.

The residents claim that a lot of the problems they face stem from an increase in large real estate projects in the area, as when projects are being executed, roads are dug up and not repaired properly. They also suspect that unregulated construction is a main factor in roads being damaged frequently even after being fixed.

“We are planning a protest, if nothing happens,” one resident threatened.

That resident, who withheld his name, pointed to a spot where water was spouting through a break in the asphalt on Waterworks Road. “They don’t use shingles or anything like that when they are fixing the roads, so the road is being eaten out from underneath,” he said.

As it relates to apartment projects being undertaken in the area, the resident said the road infrastructure can’t support the developments.

Pointing to premises on Waterworks Road where heavy-duty trucks used in construction were parked, the resident said the community has no idea what the plans for the location are, and is opposed to any more major construction projects at this time. Attempts have been made by members of the community to acquire information from the authorities about the developers’ plans, but they have hit a roadblock, having been told by authorities that they can get a copy of the documents in 60 days. However, this time frame poses a problem for the residents who said they are aware that under the law, they have a limited period in which to file an objection to any proposed construction projects.

In a letter recently penned by residents, which the

Observer saw, the residents said, “For nearly two years, residents of Broadway Close, Broadway Road, Sharrow Drive, and Waterworks Road in Kingston 8 have endured a slow-motion disaster. A developer dug up their roads to lay sewer pipes, left the reinstatement in a dangerously substandard condition, and vanished — while the authorities responsible for enforcing the law have failed to act. The result is that a car recently hit a sinkhole in a patched section and got stuck. Inferior patching work has crumbled under the weight of daily traffic. And residents are left asking a question that echoes across Jamaica: why are the laws on the books not being enforced?”

It continued: “The Parochial Roads Act gives the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) clear and unequivocal authority over parochial roads like Broadway Road and Waterworks Road. It requires any developer digging up a public road to obtain a road-opening permit and provide a refundable security deposit — money held by the KSAMC to ensure that if the developer fails to properly restore the road, the corporation can do the job using those funds,” the letter stated.

“…On Broadway Road and Waterworks Road, the developer dug up the roads, laid pipes, and left behind inferior patching that has deteriorated into sinkholes and dangerous driving conditions. The KSAMC’s preliminary finding, confirmed by Member of Parliament for the area Delano Seiveright, is clear.

“But where is the accountability? If [a security deposit] was obtained [from the developer], why hasn’t it been used to fix the roads? If none was obtained, why was the developer allowed to dig up public roads without providing the required guarantee?“

Seiveright, meanwhile, said he shared the frustration of residents, stating that their concerns are legitimate and that he has been lobbying on their behalf for a remedy.

“It is important to note that the Waterworks issue pre-dates my election as Member of Parliament [for St Andrew North Central],“ he pointed out. ”Since taking office, I have met repeatedly with officials at the highest levels of the Ministry of Water, the National Water Commission (NWC), KSAMC, and the National Environment and Planning Agency, carried out several site visits and technical walk-throughs, and spoken directly with many affected residents. I also escalated the matter to Minister [of Water] Matthew Samuda.“

He said the situation in Waterworks centres on corrective works following a private developer’s sewer project in the area. He added that while the developer is at the heart of this debacle, he is pleased that KSAMC and the NWC are now working assiduously to deliver a proper resolution.

Seiveright said his advocacy has also helped to prompt a broader review of how these projects are supervised, with stronger oversight and policy improvements now being actively pursued.

“I am aware of similar issues in other communities. More broadly, residents have raised concerns about overdevelopment, infrastructure capacity and protecting community character. I share those concerns. Development must be responsible, properly planned and supported by adequate infrastructure. I have consistently conveyed residents’ views to the relevant authorities and have encouraged stronger community organisation,“ he explained.

“The Orange Grove/Bridgemount Citizens’ Association is an excellent example of the kind of united, constructive leadership that helps communities achieve results. I will continue to press vigorously for better communication with residents, stronger enforcement where necessary, and practical solutions that protect both our communities and their quality of life,” he said.

World.title: Saint International’s Fashion Face of the Caribbean set for August 29
World.content:
From left: Deiwight Peters, founder, CEO of Saint International; model Kai Newman; Member of Parliament for St Andrew Eastern and Minister of Finance Fayval Williams, and Saint International model Carolyn Sangster.Samuel Edie

For 26 years Saint International has been the leading model agency across the region, unearthing new talent each year who have gone on to achieve success on the international fashion scene.

A new set of model hopefuls are poised for international success after more than 30 were selected on Sunday, July 26 during a Saint International Community Model Search, which took place at Jamaica College.

This was the fifth model search to have taken place this year and, according to Saint International boss Deiwight Peters, this one was the biggest thus far.

“This model search is the last in the series, and we’ve had five so far. I do believe this was the biggest one; not only in terms of the size of the turnout, but certainly the faces that turned out, they were remarkable. I do feel strongly that on August 29, when we have the finals of the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition (for both male and female), several of these new discoveries will go on to bigger things,” Peters told the Jamaica Observer shortly after the model search ended.

“We have several top agencies who will be coming in for the event, who are representing the major fashion markets in New York, London, Milan, Paris, Germany, and even Spain and they are just excited to be coming to Jamaica,” shared Peters.

Member of Parliament for St Andrew Eastern and Minister of Finance and the Public Service Fayval Williams, who was in attendance at the model search, heaped praises on Peters.

“Well, I was impressed to see the young people come out for the model search because I know there is still talent all over Jamaica. Deiwight is a very reputable person, his agency has an impressive track record, and I have no doubt that several of these model hopefuls here today will become stars of tomorrow under Deiwight’s guidance,” Williams told the Observer.

Peters shared that the minister’s presence validated the work that the agency has been doing over the years.

“I think that her turning up validated what we do and the purpose of the model search. She knows the success stories of Saint International. A big thank you to the Jamaica College family for hosting us, Mr Wayne Robinson, the principal, and the team,” he said.

Kai Newman, one of Saint International’s successful models, was in attendance at the model search to encourage the newbies.

“I just flew back to Jamaica so I said why not come here and meet some of the future stars and give them some advice, a little inspiration, and motivation. I just want them to believe in Deiwight, believe in Saint International, and to just be their authentic self,” Newman, who was discovered by Peters the age of 14 while walking on the street.

Newman has walked for designers including Burberry, Tommy Hilfiger, Chanel, Gucci, Calvin Klein, Prada, Bottega, among others.

Speaking on the Fashion Face of the Caribbean competition in August, Peters shared that more than 150 models from Jamaica, Canada, United States, Europe, several Caribbean countries including Guyana, will participate.

“We have roughly 150 models who will be participating in the Fashion Face of the Caribbean and they are coming from all over the world. It’s going to be awesome,” he said.

World.title: ‘Thrilled’ 76ers confirm James signing, eye NBA title run
World.content:
Lebron James Photo: AFP

NEW YORK, United States (AFP) — LeBron James has signed a contract to play for the Philadelphia 76ers, the team announced Monday, with managing owner Josh Harris “thrilled” about chances for their first NBA title since 1983.

James announced on Friday he would play for the Sixers on a two-year deal worth US$8 million, ending a weeks-long mystery over the 41-year-old superstar’s future, but the 76ers had no comment throughout the weekend.

“I am thrilled to welcome LeBron James to the Philadelphia 76ers,” ownership managing partner Harris said in a statement. “One of the greatest players in NBA history and one of the best athletes ever, his accomplishments are iconic.”

James, the NBA’s all-time scoring leader set to begin his record 24th campaign in October, is a four-time NBA champion and four-time NBA Most Valuable Player.

After winning two titles with Miami, another with hometown club Cleveland and his most recent with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2020, James could become the first NBA player to win crowns with four different teams.

James, a three-time Olympic champion and 22-time NBA All-Star, joins a Sixers roster filled with NBA stars in hopes of bringing Philadelphia an NBA title for the first time since Julius Erving led the club to the crown 43 years ago.

“I cannot wait to see LeBron alongside Jaylen Brown, VJ Edgecombe, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and our talented roster as we work to deliver a championship for Philly,” Harris said.

“To LeBron and his family: we are grateful you chose the 76ers, and look forward to this next chapter of your legendary career. Welcome to the 76ers!”

James has career averages of 26.8 points, 7.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 1.5 steals over 1,622 games.

Philadelphia 76ers president of basketball operations Mike Gansey, an Ohio high school rival of James on the court, expects the legend will boost the club and the community.

“There’s no doubt LeBron is one of the greatest players to ever play the game of basketball and there are no words to measure the impact he’ll have on this organisation,” Gansey said.

“I’ve had the pleasure of knowing LeBron since high school and have seen the high-level impact he has produced at every stop of his basketball journey. He is a consummate professional, the ultimate competitor, and a tireless worker.

“But he’s also an incredible person with natural leadership traits, a family man, and someone who possesses unwavering commitment to community and those around him. We couldn’t be happier that he’s officially here.”

The 76ers posted a photo on social media of a James jersey, keeping his tradition number 23 with his new club, hanging in a locker with a crown on a shelf inside it, a nod toward “King James” being with the Sixers.

James has taken teams into the NBA play-offs 19 times, matching a league record, with post-season averages of 28.2 points, 8.9 rebounds, 7.2 assists, 1.7 steals and 1.0 blocked shots over 302 games.

In June, James announced he was leaving the Lakers and numerous clubs were seen as contenders to become his new home, including Miami, Cleveland, Golden State and Minnesota as well as the 76ers.

Philadelphia swung a deal with Boston three weeks ago for Brown, sending Paul George to the Celtics, and together with centre Embiid and top guards Maxey and Edgecombe they provided a line-up too good for James to pass up in his quest for a fifth NBA title.

“I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fan base and start this incredible journey one last time,” James posted on X Friday.

World.title: DOUBLE JOY!
World.content:
DEMARIO Prince says a talk with his coach after the first round got his mind back where it was supposed to be, leading him to win the gold medal in the 110m hurdles on Monday’s first day of track and field at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland.

Jamaica won two gold medals on the day as, minutes before Prince’s run, Romaine Beckford won the men’s high jump. Beckford’s leap to clear 2.25m brought Jamaica’s second gold in the event at the games and first in 68 years.

Prince, the fourth-straight Jamaican and fifth in the last six editions to win the 110m gold medal, ran 13.17 seconds (0.4m/s) to claim his first major global medal.

Prince, who was fourth in the 60m hurdles at the World Athletics Indoor Championships in March, was delighted with the win. “This means a lot. You know, that was the aim coming into the Commonwealth Games. You know, just to get the gold medal, do it for myself, my family, and the fans. So yeah, I’m very, very pleased, very happy with the win,” Prince told the Jamaica Observer.

The sprint hurdler said he believes this is the start of good things to come.

“I feel like I can still give more and still wrap up more gold medals,” he said, noting that he had not been happy with his first round race in which he placed second.

“I was more confident going into the final, I just had to go back in the mindset to know that I can go out there and execute as I was not pleased with the prelims. I spoke to coach Ben (Dalton) and he told me not to worry about anything, he told me that I can do this. It is a regular thing for me to go out and execute and go get the medal for Jamaica,” Prince said.

England’s Samuel Bennett ran a personal best 13.30 for the silver medal and Milan Trajkvoc clocked a season’s best 12.32 to deliver Cyprus’ first medal in the event. Jamaica’s Jerome Campbell was sixth in 13.86.

Beckford, who was eighth in 2022 and failed to clear the first height at last year’s World Athletics Championships, became the first Jamaican man to win the event since 1958 when Ernle Haisley set a then Commonwealth Games record 2.06m to capture gold.

India’s Sarvesh Anil Kushare, who also cleared 2.25m, took the silver medal. England’s NCAA champion Kimani Jack was third with 2.20m.

Two-time World Indoor bronze medallist Raymond Richards just missed a medal, placing fourth also with 2.20m.

Jamaica will hope to add more medals today with athletes qualified for several finals, including in the men’s and women’s 100m.

Women’s high jump defending champion Lamara Distin, former men’s 400m world champion Antonio Watson and 800m national champion Navasky Anderson are among those set to their first entry at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

Former national champion Rohan Watson advanced to Tuesday’s semi-final of the men’s 100m after he won his first round race in 10.13 (1.5m/s).

In the semi-final he is to be joined by Ackeem Blake who drew a bye.

Also advancing were the Ghanaian pair of Benjamin Azamati and Abdul-Rasheed Saminu, as well as Jeremiah Azu of Wales and Favour Ashe of Nigeria.

Both Jamaican entries in the female 100m, Jonielle Smith and Jodean Williams, both of whom had byes, will join the action in the semi-finals.

Former World Athletics champion Tajay Gayle led the qualifying for Wednesday’s final of the men’s long jump with 8.10m (0.1m/s). He is to be joined by Jordan Turner who had a wind-aided 7.84m (4.2m/s).

Gayle, who have won medals at the last two major global championships, had a wind-aided 7.73m (3.3m/s) and 7.40m (1.0m/s) before his big mark.

Turner was was third in his group, behind Indian Sreeshankar’s effort of 8.01m (2.0m/s) and Australian Christopher Mitrevski’s mark of 7.89m (1.8m/s).

National champion Kelly Ann Beckford (2:01.63 minutes) and Adelle Tracey (2:02.58) advanced to Wednesday’s semi-finals of the women’s 800m.

Beckford booked an automatic spot after placing third in her first-round heat behind pre-championships favourite Lillian Odira of Kenya who ran 2:01.05. Isabelle Boffey of Wales clocked 2:01.53.

Tracey advanced on time after she was fourth in her first round race, just outside the automatic qualifying places. Australia’s Sarah Billings won with 2:01.51, followed by Botswana’s Oratile Nowe (2:02.11) and Kenya’s Janet Jepkemoi (2:02.30).

Nayoka Clunis qualified for Tuesday’s women’s hammer throw final, her first major global final. She threw 64.84m in the third round, eighth best of the day.

Distin could be pushed hard in her title defence with the likes of the in-form Australian pair of Eleanor Patterson and Nicola Olyslagers, as well as former NCAA champion Temitope Simbiat Adeshina of Nigeria all ranked ahead of her going into the championships.

The Sweden-based Distin has had a season’s best 1.96m, set indoors in February and has cleared 1.94m outdoors.

Navasky Anderson will be hoping to get back to the final of the men’s 800m after he finished fifth four years ago in Birmingham, England.

Since shocking the track and field world with his gold medal in the men’s 400m in Hungary in 2023, Watson has been through some lean years, failing to get past the semis in Tokyo, Japan, last year. But he has been improving through this season.

Watson will be accompanied by Delano Kennedy and Zandrion Barnes as they seek places in the men’s 400m semi-finals.

Leah Anderson and Shana Kaye Anderson are to line up in the women’s 400m first round.

World.title: Wedding Content Creators
World.content:
A wedding content creator documents your day as it unfolds, using a smartphone to capture raw, candid moments.

Not long ago, every wedding media team consisted of a photographer and videographer. Today, there’s a new professional joining the line-up — the wedding content creator.

If you’ve spent any time on Instagram or TikTok, you’ve probably seen the rise of behind-the-scenes wedding clips, emotional first looks, candid bridal party moments, and beautifully edited reels appearing within hours of the celebration. That’s the work of a wedding content creator.

This person is responsible for capturing authentic, real-time moments throughout the day, usually using a smartphone. The focus isn’t producing a cinematic wedding film or a gallery of professionally edited images. Instead, the wedding content creator documents the experience as it unfolds, creating vertical videos, candid clips, and social-ready content that couples can relive and share almost immediately.

So how are they different from a videographer? A videographer tells the story of your wedding through carefully planned shots, professional cameras, audio equipment, lighting, and expert editing. The result is a timeless wedding film that beautifully documents your ceremony, speeches, and celebration.

A content creator, on the other hand, captures the moments in-between — the laughter while getting ready, your mother’s emotional reaction as she helps you into your dress, the bridesmaids dancing in the suite, your guests’ excitement before the ceremony, or your partner’s nervous smile just before walking down the aisle. These are often the unscripted moments that couples cherish most because they reflect how the day actually felt.

Each has its advantages. A videographer delivers polished, high-quality storytelling that you’ll treasure for decades. The downside is that editing takes time, so your finished film may not arrive for several weeks or even months.

A content creator provides immediate gratification. Many deliver raw footage within 24 hours and edited reels shortly after, allowing couples to relive their day while the emotions are still fresh. However, smartphone footage is not intended to replace the production quality of professional videography.

If your budget allows, having both is the ideal combination.

The videographer preserves your wedding as a timeless film, while the content creator documents the emotion, spontaneity, and behind-the-scenes memories that often never make it into the final edit. Together, they create a complete story — one that is beautifully produced and deeply personal.

If you must choose one, let your priorities guide the decision. If preserving your vows, speeches, and ceremony in cinematic quality is more important, invest in a professional videographer. If you value candid moments, quick delivery, and social-media-ready memories, a content creator may be the better fit.

Whichever you choose, remember that great wedding content isn’t about following trends or chasing viral moments. The best professionals take the time to understand your personalities, your priorities, and the atmosphere you want to create. They know when to step in for a memorable shot and, just as importantly, when to step back and quietly capture the genuine interactions unfolding around them.

Because the most meaningful wedding memories aren’t always the ones you planned. They’re the fleeting glances, unexpected laughter, happy tears, and quiet moments that happen in-between.

At the end of the day, strong wedding content isn’t simply about documenting what happened, it’s about preserving how your wedding day felt — and that’s a memory worth investing in.

World.title: Public Advisory: Fraudulent Website Alert
World.content:
Jamaica Observer Limited is advising the public of an unauthorised and deceptive website that is unlawfully using our name, logo, and other brand elements to imitate our official platform and mislead individuals.

We are aware that a fabricated article is being circulated on social media claiming to originate from the Jamaica Observer.

The article references former Cabinet minister Lisa Hanna and a purported investment platform, and it improperly uses the image and likeness of the public figure, purporting to create the appearance of an endorsement or affiliation with the platform described in the article. These claims are entirely false. The website and related social media posts are fraudulent and have no connection to the Jamaica Observer. Such platforms may attempt to collect personal information, solicit payments, or otherwise misrepresent our services. How to Protect Yourself
