I found moving around in the timeline, also moving with perspective, it didn't build into a complete whole. This trend of using alternating chapters and voices — I just want Australian writers to go deep and give me the whole story without feeling the need to show that this is one person's perspective and this is another's. Just give me the total book.

CN: I was thinking about the same thing, Sarah. With so many of these novels, there's one strand of the story I like better than the other, and sometimes I'm reading one chapter faster because I want to get back to the bit I like. That's a danger with this type of writing, right? It's the case for quite a few books on this list, that they're a little lopsided in the reading.

Little World by Josephine Rowe

Rowe's debut novel, A Loving, Faithful Animal, was longlisted for the 2017 Miles Franklin Literary Award. (Supplied: Black Inc.)

DF: This book is about a saint, but she's an unusual saint in that the Vatican don't seem to be aware of her. It's a girl who has a body that does not decompose, and the story is about the ways in which her incorruptible saintly body and existence impact the lives of the people she comes into contact with, which include a retired engineer living near Broome in the 1950s and three women in the 70s who are travelling across Australia in a van, a lesbian couple and a woman who's a bit older called Mathilde.

The language is stunning. Josephine Rowe writes like an angel. The novel is very elliptical; how willing the reader is to sit with its suggestive aspects will determine how much they get out of it.

For me, the biggest impact the novel has is how very compactly, very succinctly, very beautifully Josephine Rowe reflects upon the lives of women. It's this communion between Mathilde and the saint, where they're women who are struggling with violence, both geopolitical and personal, and how they find some kind of solace in one another.

KE: I like the fact that it's such an odd take on an Australian history. I thought it was so fresh and surprising and odd and restrained, in a good way.

It worked as a really short novel. If it had been a sprawling 400-page novel doing this, taking all these perspectives, I think I would've needed to lie down. But having it compressed and poetic like this worked for me.

CN: It works for me too. Anyone who can put that much into 130 pages is just so clever. I think it's a pretty perfect little object.

You Must Remember This by Sean Wilson

You Must Remember This started out as a play inspired by Wilson's observations of his grandmother's experience of dementia. (Supplied: Simon & Schuster)

CN: We're with a character called Grace. She is an elderly woman and at the start of the book, we're remembering things with her when, all of a sudden, we look down with her at her feet and we realise that she is walking along a highway, there are cars whizzing by, it's in the middle of the night and she had no idea how she got there.

We realise this is a character with Alzheimer's disease, and we are with her as time and memory shifts. There are some really clever ways that Sean Wilson does this, including starting the book at chapter 10, and the chapters shift as we move around in time and Grace's memory.

We have scenes in the modern day where her daughter is trying to connect with her and is getting increasingly frustrated. But we also go back to Grace's childhood in Perth, which we learn was incredibly difficult, with an alcoholic, cruel mother.

This is a really short, beautiful book that tells the story of dementia in a really beautiful and important way, because I don't think there's a lot of fiction that tries to take dementia head on and give the characters respect and time to really explore what it might be like to experience it.

SL: I felt like its biggest strength was taking us into the confusing world of a person with dementia but giving that person a history and a present and situating them in a place, not just disregarding them because they no longer make sense to the outside world.

CN: Again, we've got that alternating chapter approach, with Grace in the present day and going back to different parts of her story. Once again, I was more drawn to the stuff in the past than the present day.

The character of her mother, Annie, reminded me of Dolly Pickles from Cloudstreet: this very loud, once beautiful and now cruel alcoholic woman.

She was such a strong character that at times I felt she wanted to become our main character. I wanted more of Annie.

SL: I thought the writing was exquisite. Being at sea is something I don't typically enjoy, but I liked being at sea with Grace and discovering what's going on with her. I felt safe in the author's hands and trusted that he was going to take me somewhere.

I found it a very satisfying read for those reasons. Claire says that Little World was a perfect book — for me, You Must Remember This was a perfect nugget of a book. It didn't overextend itself and while the remembrances of the past were very vibrant and alive, I felt the danger of Grace's present situation very much.

CN: It's another book that doesn't overstay its welcome, much like Little World and My Heart at Evening. I think Australian fiction can get really shaggy and sometimes needs another edit and to see some books that actually tell the story they need to tell and then finish is really lovely.

Snubs, surprises and tips

CN: I would have loved to have seen Toni Jordan make the shortlist for her novel Tenderfoot. I think it's the best novel she's ever written.

I still think this is an excellent list. I don't know what will win but I would enjoy it if First Name Second Name won just for being weird and wonderful.

DF: My snub is Olivia De Zilva's Plastic Budgie, put out by Pink Shorts Press, a great small publisher. It reminded me of [American novelist] Lynne Tillman who I adore. Elegy, Southwest by Madeleine Watts was quite moving and I would have also liked to see that on the shortlist.

Listen to ABC RN's The Bookshelf The latest and best fiction reviewed by a team of dedicated bibliophiles.

The winner I think is going to be Omar Musa. Prize judging tends to be splitting the difference between books people love and books they can agree upon. I don't know what the judges will love, but I think they'll probably agree upon Omar Musa.

I think Konrad Muller should win. It was just such a wow debut.

SL: I would have liked to see Charlotte McConnaghy's Wild Dark Shore on the list — it's nice to see Miles Franklin being a little bit more popular and I really loved that book.

While I'd like You Must Remember This to win, I also think Fierceland will win.

KE: I would love to see My Heart at Evening win, but I can never guess these things. I think it's a really interesting shortlist.

World.title: Fan fault shuts Sydney's M5 in morning rush, causing 10km of traffic chaos
World.content:
Traffic on the M5 motorway has been backed up for more than 10 kilometres due to the closure of city-bound lanes on the M5.

Transurban, which operates the road, closed the tunnel earlier this morning in order to repair a ventilator fan.

Aerial footage and the Live Traffic website show cars backed up from the closure point near Beverly Hills, all the way to Milperra.

Transport for New South Wales coordinator-general Howard Collins urged drivers to avoid the area as the delays are not expected to be resolved until after the morning peak.

"I'd ask people, if you don't need to travel in that area, maybe stay at home or do something different and if you do need to travel, take your time, be patient with people," Mr Collins said.

He said diversions were in place via King Georges Road and Stoney Creek Road, and the M8 is open, but those roads were also heavily congested.

Mr Collins said Transurban crews were at the site working to repair the fan, work which would require a crane.

"It's the physical nature of this fan, which needs to be removed, does negate anyone using the tunnel," he said.

"The engineers are all down there, they're working as hard as they can … but it's going to take time.

"Obviously this was an undiscovered fault which they found overnight."

World.title: Grenades, guns and drugs worth millions seized from Sydney 'gang safehouse'
World.content:
Drugs and a number of weapons including grenades have been seized during a police raid on an alleged safe house in Sydney's south-west.

Taskforce Falcon detectives, who investigate organised crime, made the discovery while carrying out a firearm prohibition order compliance check at a Glenfield home about 9am on Tuesday morning.

NSW Police seized six grenades, three semi-automatic assault rifles, four shotguns, a pistol, firearm parts, and more than 1,000 rounds of ammunition.

Police found six grenades at the Glenfield property. (Supplied: NSW Police)

A number of drugs were also found, including 15 kilograms of cannabis and 6kg of cocaine.

Police estimate the potential street value of the drugs is worth about $3 million.

Electronic devices and $9,000 cash were also located.

A man and a woman both aged 26 were arrested at the address and taken to Campbelltown Police Station.

The 26-year-old man arrested has been denied bail. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The man was charged with 27 offences including possessing more than three unregistered firearms without licence/permit, and knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime.

He has been refused bail and is expected to appear in court on Wednesday.

A 26-year-old woman has been taken to Campbelltown Police Station. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The woman was charged with assisting at a drug premises.

She was granted bail and is expected to go before the court on August 27.

World.title: 'The Aussies are on fire' on a night where that should've been impossible
World.content:
In the land of lochs, the announcer at Scotstoun Stadium couldn't figure out the first half of his name, but Lachlan Kennedy's performance on a sodden night in Glasgow ensured Australia will never forget it.

The weather on Tuesday night couldn't have been much more Scottish.

It was teeming basically all night, to the point the women's high jump final was halted for 45 minutes and the women's hammer throw probably should have been.

There were only two brief windows when the rain turned from a downpour to a drizzle, and it just so happened to be the moments "Lacklan" Kennedy was welcomed to the newly laid blue track.

The support crew was working overtime to make things vaguely manageable. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

It sounds like the sort of apocryphal tale told about Don Bradman in an era before the footage existed to prove your grandad was lying to you.

But it really happened.

To be clear, it wasn't dry, but no wetter than the night in March when he beat rising superstar Gout Gout in the 200m at the Maurie Plant Meet.

That established him once again as not just a fast runner, but a man capable of performing under the most intense pressure. A man plying his trade against a boy still figuring his out.

And Kennedy did it again on the biggest stage, winning Australia's first men's 100 metres medal at the Commonwealth Games with silver behind Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme on the second night of an athletics program that has been backed to deliver so much for Australia.

After not running a heat, Lachie Kennedy came straight out and made a statement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's all about rising to the occasion, I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most," Kennedy said.

"That's what we've been training for all season. We've all been planning for this competition here and my coach has clearly outdone himself."

It seems extreme to say he obliterated the national record of Patrick Johnson by taking it from 9.93 down to 9.85, but 0.08 of a second means something different to folks like Kennedy than it does us mere mortals.

In the 58 years since Jim Hines broke the 10-second barrier in the 100 metres, only 232 more have people dipped into single digits.

The margins are so fine in the jewel in the athletics crown that there have been 1,550 legal runs in 0.42 of a second between 10 flat and Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58.

Most are from the United States, Jamaica and spread across Africa, and just two from Australia, with Kennedy the only one since 2003.

Kennedy stands alone in some respects, but is proud to be part of a pack pushing each other towards greatness.

Gout's rise trained a spotlight on the team, whose performances with that attention have proved it warranted.

"Aussie track is clearly in the best spot it's ever been, our team is so strong … We're in a real golden age," Kennedy said.

That was clearly evident as Kennedy — after running alongside compatriot Eddie Nketia, who finished sixth in the final after laying down a PB of 10.03 in the semis — was still talking to the media in the mixed zone when Torrie Lewis won bronze in the women's final.

Loading...

"The Aussies are on fire," Kennedy said as he cheered Lewis on to the team's third of six medals on the night.

Lewis also set a new national record, but rather than breaking a record that had stood for 23 years, hers had barely stood for 23 hours.

Lewis's 10.99 in the women's final came after her 11 flat in the semi, which lowered her own record of 11.04 from a week prior.

All in an event she wasn't even sure she wanted to compete in.

Torrie Lewis followed Lachie Kennedy into the history books. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Lewis is one of the controversial automatic qualifiers into the semis of her pet 200m event, where she'll be hoping for more silver (or better) ware before the relays kick off in the ultimate representation of what this team can do.

"I have a day off tomorrow, luckily with the bye, then Thursday see how I pull up for the semifinal and hopefully I can do something special there as well," she said.

Lewis and Kennedy were the headlines due to Australia's historic lack of truly exceptional flat sprint talent since the days of Raelene Boyle.

We've jumped at shadows and sometimes athletes have failed to truly emerge from them, while field sensations have been consistently brilliant.

They were again on Tuesday night: Eleanor Patterson and Nicola Olyslagers went 1-2 to continue their impossibly consistent excellence in the high jump, and 22-year-old Lara Roberts broke through for her first major international medal.

Meanwhile, back on the track Ky Robinson kicked off the stunning hour and a half with victory in the 10,000m

Australian athletics has had a number of these special nights of late, so much so that it risks becoming the expected norm.

Australians have become so used to success in the pool that we have become somewhat blasé about the expected brilliance of our aquatic elite, but for now, on relatively dry land in Scotstoun there really is no other word for it.

That was special.

World.title: Fresh DNA evidence in 'Echo Point Man' cold case
World.content:
Police hope fresh DNA evidence will help investigators crack a more than two-decades-old cold case in the NSW Blue Mountains.

On June 4, 2004, the body of a man was found in bushland at Echo Point in Katoomba.

Despite extensive inquiries over the past 22 years, police have never been able to identify him.

The man's body was found in 2004 in Katoomba. (Supplied: Skull Forensics via NSW Police)

Advanced DNA analysis has now revealed so-called Echo Point Man likely had Latvian ancestry.

Police also now say he was more than 60 years old.

At the time he was found, Echo Point Man had been wearing a blue button-up shirt, a red cardigan, a cream jacket, blue corduroy pants, a black belt, and brown work boots.

Previously released images of a 3D facial reconstruction indicated he was likely Caucasian, with light grey hair and frontal baldness.

This backpack was found on the man, police say. (Supplied: NSW Police )

He was about 178cm tall and of medium build.

A note linked to the man also led detectives to believe he had been suffering significant eyesight problems at the time of his death.

Despite earlier appeals, no-one has ever come forward to say they recognised him.

A note linked to the man said the author was "unable to work any longer" due to poor eyesight. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Blue Mountains Police Area Command Superintendent John Nelson said they hope releasing the new information on Echo Point Man's ancestry will help provide his team with leads.

"We are now appealing to anyone with information about a man missing since early 2000s, possibly with Latvian or Middle European heritage, to contact police," he said in a statement.

Latvian community asked to help 'solve puzzle'

Superintendent Nelson told 2GB police were also calling on members of Australia's Latvian community to provide DNA samples, in the hopes it would help detectives "solve the puzzle".

"He may have migrated anywhere from the 1950s right through to the early 2000s ... maybe he's been a friend that somebody lost touch with during that period, or a long-lost uncle or a brother," he said.

A pair of scissors (right) were retrieved from the backpack. (Supplied: Skull Forensics via NSW Police)

Superintendent Nelson said a coronial inquest into his death delivered an "open finding".

He said some personal toiletries were found with his body, which suggested he might have been between homes or sleeping rough when he died.

Police do not suspect foul play.

World.title: 'My time': Young gun Southam dethrones Chalmers in 100m final
World.content:
Kyle Chalmers has been dethroned as the Commonwealth Games 100m freestyle king in Glasgow, the "Big Tuna" having been reeled in by young friend and rival Flynn Southam in a landmark changing-of-the-guard moment.

With a potential record-breaking 10th Commonwealth gold in his sights, Chalmers had his proud record of never having been beaten by an Australian in major international competition dismantled by 21-year-old Southam in the Tollcross pool.

Southam's glory, fuelled by indignation at how he'd been somewhat dismissed as just a relay workhorse, set the tone for yet another medal-laden session of Dolphins' domination on the penultimate night of the program.

Jenna Forrester sealed her own golden treble in a remarkable breakthrough meet, adding a thrilling 200m individual medley triumph to the surprise 200m backstroke and 400m IM titles she'd already annexed.

And the night kicked off with 22-year-old Queenslander Kirralee Hayes taking the para gold medal in the 50m freestyle S13 final, and another Australian, Jenna Jones, taking bronze.

But Southam's win took pride of place, the young Fremantle-born, NSW-raised prospect finally fulfilling his potential as the most likely successor to "King Kyle", clocking a searing 47.13 seconds to bronze medallist Chalmers' 47.74. The pair were split by Welshman Matt Richards (47.64).

"Me and Kyle have utmost respect for one another. But it's my time to shine, and I know that," boomed Southam.

"I've been due for this, and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here as a little boy — but now I'm a man, and I belong here."

Flynn Southam says the Commonwealth Games are his breakout meet after winning gold in the men's 100m freestyle. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For Chalmers, though, cheered on by his wife, Norwegian international swimmer Ingeborg Loyning and baby daughter Astrid, there was a mixture of frustration that he couldn't land the 10th gold and 12th medal that would have taken him past the great Ian Thorpe as Australia's most successful men's swimmer ever at the Games.

Port Lincoln's 28-year-old maestro is likely to still have a chance, though, in the 50m butterfly final on the final day of competition in what could be his final appearance at the Games.

Admitting that he knew the passing-of-the-baton moment was inevitably coming at some point soon, Chalmers had hoped to delay it but was happy to tip his hat to the young gun after being the first to congratulate him.

"I'm completely fine with it," Chalmers said.

"I'd rather be in the race for that to happen than be retired and seeing them swim faster than maybe what… well, he hasn't quite got me just yet, but it's very close to what my best ever was.

"When we were able to sit in the medal presentation, I really said, 'You know, this is your moment. I'm so proud of you, enjoy your moment, enjoy singing the anthem.'

"I truly am so proud of him."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Southam had signalled his intentions at the start of the week when he clocked a sizzling lead-off relay leg of 47.09, which was just a hundredth of a second slower than Chalmers' all-time best and quicker than the South Australian star's 2026 best by half a second.

"It's pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my success only comes from relays, and that's really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world," said Southam.

"Doubt always comes up, I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it's about being able to turn that voice down and believing in yourself.

"I have Australia on my cap, I don't have just my name, so it's bigger than me."

Another medal came Australia's way with William Petric taking silver in the 400m individual medley behind New Zealand's double champion Lewis Clareburt.

AAP

World.title: Live: Victorian premier addresses media a day after taking leadership
World.content:
Mr Carroll is taking questions from reporters on the back of yesterday's events and his decision to announce a royal commission into the construction sector.

The feed from the Kmart basement is very patchy so we're not hearing everything that is being said, but Mr Carroll has reiterated some of his comments yesterday on the RC.

"I am going to run a disciplined, proper cabinet process," he says.

The premier says he will schedule a cabinet meeting as soon as he can to establish the settings for the royal commission.

World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Premier Ben Carroll mulls cabinet appointments following Jacinta Allan’s resignation
World.content:
Former Labor premier Steve Bracks says Jacinta Allan should have called a royal commission into the construction sector but praised new Premier Ben Carroll for quickly announcing one.

“I know that she [Allan] felt that a royal commission wouldn’t achieve the aims that people thought it would,” Bracks just told ABC Radio National, “but you know that’s water under the bridge now, and essentially, what has happened is that the new premier, Ben Carroll, has moved very quickly, very effectively.”

World.title: Records tumble, sprinters star – and the rest. This was Australia’s greatest ever night in athletics
World.content:
Analysis SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games Records tumble, sprinters star – and the rest. This was Australia’s greatest ever night in athletics Michael Gleeson July 29, 2026 — 8:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Australia has spoken of its new golden age of athletics. This was its golden night. Sport is vulnerable to hyperbole, but it is not hyperbolic to say Tuesday night at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow was possibly the greatest Australia has ever had in track and field. Lachlan Kennedy and his newly minted Australian record. Getty Certainly it was in sprinting. And it was certainly the best night of athletics you probably slept through. Lachlan Kennedy broke not only 10 seconds in the men’s 100 metres, but 9.9s. He broke the national record, won Commonwealth silver and was annoyed it wasn’t gold. Torrie Lewis broke 11 seconds in the women’s 100m and won bronze.



Ky Robinson matched Rose Davies’ effort from the night before and won 10,000m gold. Eleanor Patterson and Nicola Olyslagers won gold and silver, respectively, in the high jump. While that no longer counts as a news story because they always share a podium and the question is only who takes the higher step, Patterson crowned herself a Glasgow queen. Her victory matched the Commonwealth gold she won in Scotland 12 years ago as a 17-year-old schoolgirl. Head-to-head, Patterson and Olyslagers have won 29 times each and tied one other time. It is a rivalry. Torrie Lewis was all smiles after running sub-11 seconds in the 100m. AP And from nowhere, Lara Roberts won a hammer throw bronze medal. The hammer! When does Australia ever win a hammer medal? Six medals in one night is unprecedented. These were not school sports efforts, beating up on under-strength fields. The times these athletes ran in the sprints, and the runners they went stride for stride with, are world standard.



Sub-10 and -11 times put any sprinter in the mix at the line in any level of event. Kayinsola Ajayi, whom Kennedy edged out for silver in a photo finish, ran 9.84s only a week ago and an illegal 9.72 a week before that. Gold medallist in the 10,000m, Robinson, was fourth at the world championships in the 5000m last year. He is the reigning NCAA champion over five and 10km in the US college system. And this was without teen sprint sensation Gout Gout. At the risk of making this a Gout story when he is not here in Scotland, the point is that he isn’t here, and his compatriots did this anyway. Australia’s greatest night of sprinting happened without the biggest name in the sport for the last year competing here. But then, Kennedy and Lewis are reframing the idea of the big names in athletics. The last time Australia won a men’s sprint medal, it was called the 100-yard dash and the British Empire and Commonwealth Games. Mickey Cleary won bronze that day in 1962. Sixty-four years later, Kennedy beat the man considered the fastest in the world this year, Nigeria’s Ajayi.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Chalmers has owned 100m freestyle for 10 years, but this young gun just dethroned him Kennedy becoming a 9.8s runner puts him in the frame in any meet, anywhere. At the Olympics inLA in two years’ time, he can win a medal with that sort of form, but beyond that with that sort of trend. His 9.85s in Glasgow was the fifth fastest in the world this year. “I mean, I came in here wanting to win, but second place with a big, fresh PB, it’s a pretty good consolation prize, you know,” Kennedy said. It should never have been like this. Nothing said it was a night to run fast. Hosing rain and cold, a small boutique track, thunder rumbling over the houses ringing the track. “To be able to come out here in those conditions against a field like that … I mean, it’s pride, I guess. Very proud for my country to be able to get a medal in the Comm Games,” he said.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ “It’s all about rising to the occasion. I’m a big believer in you have got to bring your best when it matters most. “I mean, my goal is always to win in everything I do, be that Olympics, Comm Games, you know, Shield meets, I don’t really care who’s out there. At the end of the day, I can only control how I run. I can’t control how the others run. So I’m gonna go out there, do my best, and aim to win everything, including Olympics.” Kennedy broke 10 seconds twice in the night – 9.94s in the semi-final then his 9.85 in the final. He is now a regular sub-10 runner, having broken through to single figures five times now. But more than that, breaking 9.9 is leaping ahead into new territory as a runner, especially to do it in unfavourable conditions. Both he and Lewis will back up for the 200m and relays at these Games. In the form they are in, more medals beckon.



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Kennedy smashes record to win silver in 100m; Southam gold leads medal rush at the pool Lewis thought she’d broken 11 seconds in her semi-final; she crossed the line and the clock had stopped at 10.98s. Moments later it was revised to 11 seconds. They have a sense of drama, the Scots. She came to the final and smashed through the 11 anyway. “I was hoping I got a medal, but I didn’t want to like, celebrate too early, just in case I got fourth or something else. But yeah, when I saw my name on the screen, I was super happy. And then to see the 10.99, I was really happy,” she said. “I’ve just had Commonwealth in my sights ever since I didn’t make the Tokyo final [at the world championships] last year. You know, at first it was to make a final, but then through the year I’ve just been like, you know, I just want to go for a medal as well. “It’s also just relief that I’ve been able to finish in one piece, and you know, it is confidence. Like you can just run through the pain and yeah, win a medal at Commonwealth.”

World.title: Ariana Grande sues over hacking campaign that leaked dozens of songs
World.content:
CultureMusicAriana Grande Ariana Grande sues over hacking campaign that leaked dozens of songs Derrick Bryson Taylor July 29, 2026 — 8:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against anonymous hackers who she said for years stole, sold and leaked dozens of unreleased songs, video footage and private images obtained through a series of account intrusions and phishing scams. The lawsuit, filed Monday in the Superior Court of California for Los Angeles County, said that some of the hacked materials have been sold on the dark web for significant sums of money or were published on social media platforms and other content transfer systems, like WeTransfer and Dropbox. Ariana Grande has sued unnamed hackers in a bid to stop them distributing unreleased music and personal photographs. Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP “Defendants also use multiple accounts, specifically designed to mask their identities, in order to publish the content they illegally accessed and stole,” the lawsuit said. No hackers were identified by name, but the singer hopes to use the complaint to “uncover the identities” of the people involved, the court papers said.



Representatives for Grande declined to comment on the lawsuit on Tuesday (US time). The filing comes amid a busy time for Grande. She’s on a world tour, with a spate of sold-out shows in Montreal this week. Her latest studio album, Petal, will be released Friday. The complaint details digital attacks dating back to 2019, when hackers obtained login credentials to a Dropbox account of a photographer with whom Grande had previously worked. In that episode, hackers accessed and downloaded unreleased photos. Then in 2020, cybercriminals hacked their way into the mobile device of a producer on Grande’s team, downloading unreleased masters, demos and footage from recording sessions, the complaint said. Three years later, hackers struck again, stealing and then leaking 45 unreleased songs. The suit also detailed two episodes in early 2024, when a digital technician fell victim to phishing scams after hackers created a fake email account and domain name impersonating a photographer. In those incidents, the hackers obtained unreleased photos.



Related Article Pop culture Australian man who ambushed Ariana Grande on red carpet jailed in Singapore “This malicious invasion of Ms Grande’s privacy and disruption of her career have caused her substantial and irreparable harm,” the complaint said, adding that no one should have to suffer such violations. Not only have the hacks caused Grande reputational harm, the complaint said, they have forced her to use significant resources to investigate the matter, take down materials published without her consent and rerecord songs. Grande seeks a trial by jury and court orders demanding the defendants turn over all private materials. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

World.title: Chalmers has owned 100m freestyle for 10 years, but this young gun just dethroned him
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Chalmers has owned 100m freestyle for 10 years, but this young gun just dethroned him Tom Decent July 29, 2026 — 8:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Not being able to beat Kyle Chalmers always ate away at Flynn Southam, a precocious young swimmer with a bright future who had never quite delivered as an individual on the international stage after bursting onto the scene in 2022. Southam was convinced an outstanding block of training since last year’s world championships in Singapore would finally allow him to topple Chalmers in the 100 metres freestyle at Australia’s selection trials last month – something no Australian had done since Cam McEvoy in 2017. Flynn Southam celebrates winning gold in the men’s 100m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games. AP He faded badly to finish second in 47.94 seconds as Chalmers chalked up another win. Southam promised himself it would not happen again, admitting afterwards he took the defeat “very personally”.



Seven weeks on, Southam ended Chalmers’ decade-long grip on the event in emphatic fashion at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow before firing back at suggestions he was merely a relay swimmer, declaring he wants to become the world’s best in the blue-riband event that his close friend has dominated for years. Flynn Southam (gold) and Kyle Chalmers (bronze) during the Australian national anthem. Getty Images As Australia equalled its record haul of 28 swimming gold medals at a Commonwealth Games with another five victories on the penultimate night in the pool, Southam officially stepped out of Chalmers’ shadow with a commanding win in a world-class time of 47.13 that further fuelled belief he can contend for an Olympic medal in Los Angeles in 2028. The 21-year-old said he would celebrate with a Great Northern beer and a fishing trip when he returned home after finally fulfilling years of promise. An eye-catching lead-off split of 47.09 in Australia’s victorious 4x100m freestyle relay on Friday – slicing 0.6 seconds off his personal best and finishing just 0.01 seconds off Chalmers’ lifetime best – only heightened expectations. But Southam backed up his pre-race declaration that he could beat the 2016 Rio Olympic champion, touching in 47.13 while Chalmers settled for third in 47.74. Wales’ Matt Richards was second in 47.64.



It was the first time Chalmers had lost a 100m freestyle final to another Australian at an international meet, prompting the 28-year-old to openly question whether he would make it to the Los Angeles Olympics as he balances elite swimming with life as a new father. “It’s pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my successes only came from relays,” Southam said. “That’s really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world. “I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it’s about being able to turn that voice down. If I swam my game plan, no one was going to beat me. “I’ve been doing stuff in training that I know only a couple of people in the world can do better than me. I’ve got the utmost respect for Kyle and everything he has accomplished. It’s my time to shine and I am here to stay.”



Chalmers, a world champion in 2023 and silver medallist at the last Olympics in Paris two years ago, has proven over the past 10 years he is a formidable man to race, particularly with his back-end speed in second laps. His presence is like few others on the pool deck. But as Southam went out hard and took a 0.4 second lead at the turn, Chalmers realised deep down he was not going to be able to hang on. The veteran gave Southam a pat on the head after the race before telling him in the marshalling area for the medal ceremony: “This is your moment. I’m so proud of you. Enjoy singing the anthem.” There is not a hint of animosity between the pair. Chalmers was genuinely thrilled for his relay partner, even as he admitted the arrival of his newborn daughter had changed his priorities and affected his preparation this year.



Asked if the next Olympics remained a certainty, Chalmers said: “It’s never a lock for anyone, right? I’m going to be 30 years old. I would love to get to that point, but I’m also a realist and know that what is important to me now is my wife and daughter. If I don’t get to that point, I’m not going to be disappointed. I would love to get to that point but it’s going to be very challenging. Kyle Chalmers finished third in his 100m freestyle final. Getty Images “I’m not an 18-year-old kid who’s got no other things going on in life. I really have to decide what is best for my daughter and give her the best upbringing. I don’t want to be a selfish parent. I desperately want to be in LA, but yeah, you have to work that out being a parent.” For all the debate about the standard of these Commonwealth Games and Australia’s medal avalanche, do not underestimate what Southam achieved and how that will benefit his mindset. He remains well behind Pan Zhanle’s world record of 46.40 and is yet to reach the level of Romanian star David Popovici, but this performance could prove the making of him. McEvoy’s Australian record of 47.04 is in danger. “Kyle and I have the utmost respect for each other but it’s my time to shine,” Southam said. “I’ve been due for this and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here [to the UK] as a boy. Now I’m a man. I belong here.



“A want to have a sharp axe and only strike once and that’s what I did just then.” Meanwhile, Jenna Forrester (200m individual medley) and Lani Pallister (800m freestyle) claimed their third individual gold medals of the Games. Lani Pallister made it a treble of individual gold medals at the Commonwealth Games. Getty Images Pallister was satisfied with another title but disappointed by her time, while her coach Dean Boxall’s typically expressionless reaction after she clocked 8:11.12 – more than 13 seconds ahead of New Zealand’s Erika Fairweather but five seconds outside her personal best – reinforced that the focus remains firmly on Los Angeles. Kirralee Hayes also struck gold in the women’s S13 50m freestyle.



Australia rounded out the night by winning the mixed 4x100m medley relay, with Meg Harris producing a superb anchor leg to secure the Dolphins’ 28th swimming gold medal of these Games. It equalled the team’s record haul from the 2018 Gold Coast Commonwealth Games and eclipsed the 25 won in Birmingham four years ago. Whatever the arguments about the depth of competition, Australia’s dominance has been undeniable. World.title: Cockroaches, spiders and a bloody pig mask: eBay to pay $70 million to couple after threats, bizarre deliveries
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsCourts Cockroaches, spiders and a bloody pig mask: eBay to pay $70 million to couple after threats, bizarre deliveries Leah Willingham July 29, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Online giant eBay agreed to pay $US48.7million ($69.8 million) to a Massachusetts couple who said former employees of the company targeted them with threats and bizarre anonymous deliveries — including live insects, a funeral wreath and a bloody pig Halloween mask, according to settlement details. The parties reported reaching a tentative settlement in February as the case was headed to trial, but they were unable to finalise it. David and Ina Steiner asked a federal judge in June to restore the case to the trial calendar and reached a new settlement this month. In their 2021 lawsuit filed in Boston federal court, the Steiners said that the company engaged in a conspiracy to “intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorise, stalk and silence them” in order to “stifle their reporting on eBay.” Boston Globe via Getty Images The agreement with the Steiners, founders of EcommerceBytes, a newsletter covering the e-commerce industry, includes an additional $US7 million in charitable donations, including to organisations supporting First Amendment rights. The settlement contains no confidentiality provision, allowing the Steiners to discuss the case publicly. “David and I were on the same page that this settlement should and must be made public — as victims who want to prevent something like this from ever happening to anyone else, and as reporters who believe in transparency,” Ina Steiner said in an email response to questions from The Associated Press. “We hope that this case will serve as a deterrent.”



The settlement resolves more than six years of criminal and civil proceedings stemming from the harassment campaign. In their 2021 lawsuit filed in Boston federal court, the Steiners said that the company engaged in a conspiracy to “intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorise, stalk and silence them” in order to “stifle their reporting on eBay.” The Natick residents, who report on the e-commerce industry in their newsletter, said they were subjected to cyberstalking, death threats and in-person surveillance by former eBay workers. Escalating pressure Related Article Exclusive

Taxis Illegal cabbie fined $32,000 over airport touting, driving unlicensed Ina Steiner said the campaign began with threatening direct messages on social media before escalating into anonymous deliveries of live cockroaches and spiders, a funeral wreath, a bloody pig Halloween mask and a book about surviving the death of a spouse. The employees also sent pornographic magazines with David Steiner’s name to a neighbour’s home and planned to install a GPS device on the couple’s car. She said she did not initially know who was behind it or why.



“I could not conceive that a company I had been covering for the past two decades had tried to terrorise us into stopping our reporting,” she said. When the lawsuit was filed, the company said “the misconduct of these former employees was wrong,” and that it would “do what is fair and appropriate to try to address what the Steiners went through.” eBay reiterated its apology, saying, “What the Steiners were subjected to by former eBay employees in 2019 was wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened.” The company also acknowledged “the unprofessional tone in internal communications” by former CEO Devin Wenig, former chief communications officer Steve Wymer and former senior vice president Wendy Jones. The settlement resolves more than six years of criminal and civil proceedings stemming from the harassment campaign. iStock The company said the conduct “is not representative of eBay’s culture” and said it has since changed leadership and strengthened its policies, procedures and ethics training.



In 2020, federal prosecutors charged seven former eBay employees, alleging they carried out a coordinated harassment campaign against the couple after becoming angered by coverage in the couple’s online newsletter. Most of the defendants pleaded guilty to charges including conspiracy and cyberstalking and were later sentenced to prison terms or home confinement. In 2024, eBay agreed to pay a $US3 million criminal penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement with federal authorities. A ‘painful, life-changing experience’ Under the settlement, the Steiners will receive $US48.7 million in compensation, including $US46.15 million from eBay, $US2 million from former CEO Wenig, $US500,000 from former executive Jones and $US50,000 from former executive Wymer. The company will fund $US6 million in charitable contributions to various nonprofit organisations, with Wenig contributing an additional $US1 million to a charity dedicated to protecting First Amendment rights in Ina Steiner’s name.



In a statement, Steiner attorney Christopher Murphy cited the recovery amount, personal payments by former executives, a commitment for $US7 million to go to nonprofits and the absence of a confidentiality provision in a system where “wrongdoers too often hide their misdeeds by dangling compensation in front of those they victimised and trading that compensation for confidentiality or an NDA.” Related Article Updated

Recall Amazon, eBay, Kogan ordered to halt sales of potentially deadly toys Protecting journalists and publishers and deterring corporate misconduct were goals from the beginning, he said. “We believe this resolution sends a clear message that corporations and their executives cannot engage in this type of misconduct without facing significant consequences,” said Murphy, of Massachusetts-based Scalli Murphy Law. Ina Steiner said she and her husband hoped that “some good will come out of this painful, life-changing experience.” AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against anonymous hackers who she said for years stole, sold and leaked dozens of unreleased songs, video footage and private images obtained through a series of account intrusions and phishing scams. The lawsuit, filed Monday in the Superior Court of California for Los Angeles County, said that some of the hacked materials have been sold on the dark web for significant sums of money or were published on social media platforms and other content transfer systems, like WeTransfer and Dropbox. Ariana Grande has sued unnamed hackers in a bid to stop them distributing unreleased music and personal photographs. Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP “Defendants also use multiple accounts, specifically designed to mask their identities, in order to publish the content they illegally accessed and stole,” the lawsuit said. No hackers were identified by name, but the singer hopes to use the complaint to “uncover the identities” of the people involved, the court papers said.



Representatives for Grande declined to comment on the lawsuit on Tuesday (US time). The filing comes amid a busy time for Grande. She’s on a world tour, with a spate of sold-out shows in Montreal this week. Her latest studio album, Petal, will be released Friday. The complaint details digital attacks dating back to 2019, when hackers obtained login credentials to a Dropbox account of a photographer with whom Grande had previously worked. In that episode, hackers accessed and downloaded unreleased photos. Then in 2020, cybercriminals hacked their way into the mobile device of a producer on Grande’s team, downloading unreleased masters, demos and footage from recording sessions, the complaint said. Three years later, hackers struck again, stealing and then leaking 45 unreleased songs. The suit also detailed two episodes in early 2024, when a digital technician fell victim to phishing scams after hackers created a fake email account and domain name impersonating a photographer. In those incidents, the hackers obtained unreleased photos.



Related Article Pop culture Australian man who ambushed Ariana Grande on red carpet jailed in Singapore “This malicious invasion of Ms Grande’s privacy and disruption of her career have caused her substantial and irreparable harm,” the complaint said, adding that no one should have to suffer such violations. Not only have the hacks caused Grande reputational harm, the complaint said, they have forced her to use significant resources to investigate the matter, take down materials published without her consent and rerecord songs. Grande seeks a trial by jury and court orders demanding the defendants turn over all private materials. Kitty Bennett contributed research.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Chalmers has owned 100m freestyle for 10 years, but this young gun just dethroned him
World.content:
SportSwimmingCommonwealth Games Chalmers has owned 100m freestyle for 10 years, but this young gun just dethroned him Tom Decent July 29, 2026 — 8:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Glasgow: Not being able to beat Kyle Chalmers always ate away at Flynn Southam, a precocious young swimmer with a bright future who had never quite delivered as an individual on the international stage after bursting onto the scene in 2022. Southam was convinced an outstanding block of training since last year’s world championships in Singapore would finally allow him to topple Chalmers in the 100 metres freestyle at Australia’s selection trials last month – something no Australian had done since Cam McEvoy in 2017. Flynn Southam celebrates winning gold in the men’s 100m freestyle final at the Commonwealth Games. AP He faded badly to finish second in 47.94 seconds as Chalmers chalked up another win. Southam promised himself it would not happen again, admitting afterwards he took the defeat “very personally”.



Seven weeks on, Southam ended Chalmers’ decade-long grip on the event in emphatic fashion at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow before firing back at suggestions he was merely a relay swimmer, declaring he wants to become the world’s best in the blue-riband event that his close friend has dominated for years. Flynn Southam (gold) and Kyle Chalmers (bronze) during the Australian national anthem. Getty Images As Australia equalled its record haul of 28 swimming gold medals at a Commonwealth Games with another five victories on the penultimate night in the pool, Southam officially stepped out of Chalmers’ shadow with a commanding win in a world-class time of 47.13 that further fuelled belief he can contend for an Olympic medal in Los Angeles in 2028. The 21-year-old said he would celebrate with a Great Northern beer and a fishing trip when he returned home after finally fulfilling years of promise. An eye-catching lead-off split of 47.09 in Australia’s victorious 4x100m freestyle relay on Friday – slicing 0.6 seconds off his personal best and finishing just 0.01 seconds off Chalmers’ lifetime best – only heightened expectations. But Southam backed up his pre-race declaration that he could beat the 2016 Rio Olympic champion, touching in 47.13 while Chalmers settled for third in 47.74. Wales’ Matt Richards was second in 47.64.



It was the first time Chalmers had lost a 100m freestyle final to another Australian at an international meet, prompting the 28-year-old to openly question whether he would make it to the Los Angeles Olympics as he balances elite swimming with life as a new father. “It’s pretty incredible. I had a lot of people doubting me and saying my successes only came from relays,” Southam said. “That’s really pissed me off and motivated me to be the best in the world. “I was doubting myself as I was walking out, but it’s about being able to turn that voice down. If I swam my game plan, no one was going to beat me. “I’ve been doing stuff in training that I know only a couple of people in the world can do better than me. I’ve got the utmost respect for Kyle and everything he has accomplished. It’s my time to shine and I am here to stay.”



Chalmers, a world champion in 2023 and silver medallist at the last Olympics in Paris two years ago, has proven over the past 10 years he is a formidable man to race, particularly with his back-end speed in second laps. His presence is like few others on the pool deck. But as Southam went out hard and took a 0.4 second lead at the turn, Chalmers realised deep down he was not going to be able to hang on. The veteran gave Southam a pat on the head after the race before telling him in the marshalling area for the medal ceremony: “This is your moment. I’m so proud of you. Enjoy singing the anthem.” There is not a hint of animosity between the pair. Chalmers was genuinely thrilled for his relay partner, even as he admitted the arrival of his newborn daughter had changed his priorities and affected his preparation this year.



Asked if the next Olympics remained a certainty, Chalmers said: “It’s never a lock for anyone, right? I’m going to be 30 years old. I would love to get to that point, but I’m also a realist and know that what is important to me now is my wife and daughter. If I don’t get to that point, I’m not going to be disappointed. I would love to get to that point but it’s going to be very challenging. Kyle Chalmers finished third in his 100m freestyle final. Getty Images “I’m not an 18-year-old kid who’s got no other things going on in life. I really have to decide what is best for my daughter and give her the best upbringing. I don’t want to be a selfish parent. I desperately want to be in LA, but yeah, you have to work that out being a parent.” For all the debate about the standard of these Commonwealth Games and Australia’s medal avalanche, do not underestimate what Southam achieved and how that will benefit his mindset. He remains well behind Pan Zhanle’s world record of 46.40 and is yet to reach the level of Romanian star David Popovici, but this performance could prove the making of him. McEvoy’s Australian record of 47.04 is in danger. “Kyle and I have the utmost respect for each other but it’s my time to shine,” Southam said. “I’ve been due for this and this is my breakout meet. Four years ago, I came here [to the UK] as a boy. Now I’m a man. I belong here.



“A want to have a sharp axe and only strike once and that’s what I did just then.” Meanwhile, Jenna Forrester (200m individual medley) and Lani Pallister (800m freestyle) claimed their third individual gold medals of the Games. Lani Pallister made it a treble of individual gold medals at the Commonwealth Games. Getty Images Pallister was satisfied with another title but disappointed by her time, while her coach Dean Boxall’s typically expressionless reaction after she clocked 8:11.12 – more than 13 seconds ahead of New Zealand’s Erika Fairweather but five seconds outside her personal best – reinforced that the focus remains firmly on Los Angeles. Kirralee Hayes also struck gold in the women’s S13 50m freestyle.



Australia rounded out the night by winning the mixed 4x100m medley relay, with Meg Harris producing a superb anchor leg to secure the Dolphins’ 28th swimming gold medal of these Games. It equalled the team’s record haul from the 2018 Gold Coast Commonwealth Games and eclipsed the 25 won in Birmingham four years ago. Whatever the arguments about the depth of competition, Australia’s dominance has been undeniable. World.title: Cockroaches, spiders and a bloody pig mask: eBay to pay $70 million to couple after threats, bizarre deliveries
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsCourts Cockroaches, spiders and a bloody pig mask: eBay to pay $70 million to couple after threats, bizarre deliveries Leah Willingham July 29, 2026 — 8:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Online giant eBay agreed to pay $US48.7million ($69.8 million) to a Massachusetts couple who said former employees of the company targeted them with threats and bizarre anonymous deliveries — including live insects, a funeral wreath and a bloody pig Halloween mask, according to settlement details. The parties reported reaching a tentative settlement in February as the case was headed to trial, but they were unable to finalise it. David and Ina Steiner asked a federal judge in June to restore the case to the trial calendar and reached a new settlement this month. In their 2021 lawsuit filed in Boston federal court, the Steiners said that the company engaged in a conspiracy to “intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorise, stalk and silence them” in order to “stifle their reporting on eBay.” Boston Globe via Getty Images The agreement with the Steiners, founders of EcommerceBytes, a newsletter covering the e-commerce industry, includes an additional $US7 million in charitable donations, including to organisations supporting First Amendment rights. The settlement contains no confidentiality provision, allowing the Steiners to discuss the case publicly. “David and I were on the same page that this settlement should and must be made public — as victims who want to prevent something like this from ever happening to anyone else, and as reporters who believe in transparency,” Ina Steiner said in an email response to questions from The Associated Press. “We hope that this case will serve as a deterrent.”



The settlement resolves more than six years of criminal and civil proceedings stemming from the harassment campaign. In their 2021 lawsuit filed in Boston federal court, the Steiners said that the company engaged in a conspiracy to “intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorise, stalk and silence them” in order to “stifle their reporting on eBay.” The Natick residents, who report on the e-commerce industry in their newsletter, said they were subjected to cyberstalking, death threats and in-person surveillance by former eBay workers. Escalating pressure Related Article Exclusive

Taxis Illegal cabbie fined $32,000 over airport touting, driving unlicensed Ina Steiner said the campaign began with threatening direct messages on social media before escalating into anonymous deliveries of live cockroaches and spiders, a funeral wreath, a bloody pig Halloween mask and a book about surviving the death of a spouse. The employees also sent pornographic magazines with David Steiner’s name to a neighbour’s home and planned to install a GPS device on the couple’s car. She said she did not initially know who was behind it or why.



“I could not conceive that a company I had been covering for the past two decades had tried to terrorise us into stopping our reporting,” she said. When the lawsuit was filed, the company said “the misconduct of these former employees was wrong,” and that it would “do what is fair and appropriate to try to address what the Steiners went through.” eBay reiterated its apology, saying, “What the Steiners were subjected to by former eBay employees in 2019 was wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened.” The company also acknowledged “the unprofessional tone in internal communications” by former CEO Devin Wenig, former chief communications officer Steve Wymer and former senior vice president Wendy Jones. The settlement resolves more than six years of criminal and civil proceedings stemming from the harassment campaign. iStock The company said the conduct “is not representative of eBay’s culture” and said it has since changed leadership and strengthened its policies, procedures and ethics training.



In 2020, federal prosecutors charged seven former eBay employees, alleging they carried out a coordinated harassment campaign against the couple after becoming angered by coverage in the couple’s online newsletter. Most of the defendants pleaded guilty to charges including conspiracy and cyberstalking and were later sentenced to prison terms or home confinement. In 2024, eBay agreed to pay a $US3 million criminal penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement with federal authorities. A ‘painful, life-changing experience’ Under the settlement, the Steiners will receive $US48.7 million in compensation, including $US46.15 million from eBay, $US2 million from former CEO Wenig, $US500,000 from former executive Jones and $US50,000 from former executive Wymer. The company will fund $US6 million in charitable contributions to various nonprofit organisations, with Wenig contributing an additional $US1 million to a charity dedicated to protecting First Amendment rights in Ina Steiner’s name.



In a statement, Steiner attorney Christopher Murphy cited the recovery amount, personal payments by former executives, a commitment for $US7 million to go to nonprofits and the absence of a confidentiality provision in a system where “wrongdoers too often hide their misdeeds by dangling compensation in front of those they victimised and trading that compensation for confidentiality or an NDA.” Related Article Updated

Recall Amazon, eBay, Kogan ordered to halt sales of potentially deadly toys Protecting journalists and publishers and deterring corporate misconduct were goals from the beginning, he said. “We believe this resolution sends a clear message that corporations and their executives cannot engage in this type of misconduct without facing significant consequences,” said Murphy, of Massachusetts-based Scalli Murphy Law. Ina Steiner said she and her husband hoped that “some good will come out of this painful, life-changing experience.” AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Contested and congested: Pacific regional architecture gets complex, security expert says
World.content:
A Pacific geopolitical expert there is a risk that Pacific Islands' priorities and security concerns are being sidelined by increased geopolitical competition and tensions in the region.

Are there too many security alliances in the Pacific? Pacific Waves Download MP3 14m

This comes amid a growing number of security alliances being formed between Australia and Pacific countries, as well as new regional security organisations, and as China increases its footprint in the region.

Anna Powles, an associate professor at the Centre for Defence and Security Studies at Massey University, told RNZ Pacific that the already crowded regional architecture is becoming more complex, and that there is a need for clarity to ensure it is genuinely Pacific-led.

(The transcript has been edited for brevity and clarity.)

Johnny Blades: On this growing number of security or defence alliances that we are seeing in the Pacific lately, is there any precedent for this in modern times, in other regions of the world?

Anna Powles: Well, it certainly speaks to the sense of urgency on the part of, of particularly Canberra and and of course New Zealand as well, and it is a reflection of the current security environment and concerns about the trajectory of security in the region.

And where it is an interesting comparison, where we have seen the similarly, if we think about those European countries who were not NATO members and have subsequently become NATO members, such as Sweden, as a consequence of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and that impetus and the flurry of action and sense of urgency that we have seen in Europe is an interesting comparison when we consider what we are seeing now here in the Pacific.

JB: What do you see as being the risks for Pacific Island countries from these alliances?

AP: The risks are twofold. Firstly, the concern that this flurry of action, this geopolitical contestation, that we have seen really since around 2014, where we started to see it escalate - and then obviously from 2022 onwards, following the signing of the security agreement between Solomon Islands and China - the activity became that much more intensified, and the risks always are that those priorities that have been identified by Pacific Island countries themselves and laid out in declarations such as the Boe Declaration that was signed in 2018, that those concerns, those security priorities such as transnational crime, environmental security, climate change as the existential threat to Pacific peoples, to the region itself, that those issues are going to be crowded out as a consequence of geopolitical interests in the region.

We see this a great deal by the fact that even though there is discussion, there is references to Pacific Islands Forum centrality, which is similar to taking taking a spin from ASEAN centrality. There is rhetoric and the strategic narrative that the Pacific Islands Forum is at the centre of the regional architecture. But what we are seeing through this hub and spokes type model, at which Australia is very much at the centre of these regional, both bilateral and regional security and defence arrangements.

We are seeing the regional security architecture itself becoming increasingly broadened, and there are certainly concerns about what this means for the region itself, for what it means for a genuinely Pacific-led regional security architecture. The Pacific Elders group have raised these concerns themselves only a week or so ago publicly that Pacific priorities are being diluted, that Pacific priorities and strategic narratives, such as the Blue Ocean of Peace are being diluted and potentially undermined by this intensified strategic competition taking place in the region.

JB: Looking at the the Ocean of Peace Centre, which at least as it stemmed from the the Ocean of Peace Alliance signed by Fiji and Australia a few weeks ago, how do you expect the centre to operationalise the Ocean of Peace Declaration that was earlier made by forum countries?

AP: I think we are waiting to see that. Certainly, if Fiji put their hand up to to lead to host the Ocean of Peace Centre in Fiji, and it is as far as we understand, it will be as you say operationalising the Ocean of Peace Declaration, which was signed by foreign leaders at the last leaders summit in 2025. So presumably, it will seek to lead Pacific conversations on the issues that the Ocean of Peace have have identified as being critical, particularly around managing and navigating crises in the region.

There is very little information in the public domain as yet about what the mandate of the Ocean of Peace Centre will be, but we understand that it will, as you say, operationalise the Ocean of Peace Declaration.

JB: RNZ Pacific has heard some comments of concern from civil society about where the centre may be heading, or where the security alliances are heading. But your thoughts on Marco De Jong's comment about maybe regional civil society had asked for a peace centre, but maybe they got a military base instead. Is that a bit unrealistic, do you think?

AP: I think civil society are rightly concerned about the hijacking of peace building mechanisms in the region, and obviously the Pacific civil society, have been at the forefront of leading on issues such as nuclear non-proliferation, climate change, oceans governance, and so on. Their voices in this conversation is incredibly important.

Dr Anna Powles Supplied

There is there is and concern that there has been this co-opting of language in the region. We thought firstly when we started talking about the Blue Pacific and the Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, we saw the co-opting of that term Blue Pacific. And now we are also seeing this co-opting of that the Ocean of Peace language as well for strategic narrative purposes.

How that will play out again, it is less clear. Presumably, as Fiji has has put their hand up to to host the Ocean of Peace Centre, and the Ocean of Peace, of course, is very much Prime Minister Rabuka's legacy project. Hopefully, that will mean that it does maintain that regional ownership.

But specific civil society across the region have been deeply concerned that even the Ocean of Peace Declaration has not gone far enough with respect to really anchoring peace building and emphasising peace over security. Those concerns and those perspectives need to be very much part of this conversation as well.

JB: I know you have been tracking the regional security pacts and agreements that have been forged, and and also the regional security-related structures that have been established in recent times. Are they all becoming a bit complicated? Are there too many security arrangements?

AP: Well, certainly, what we are seeing increasingly is a sort of lattice work security architecture, or this highly networked security architecture in the Pacific. But it does feel that there is potentially some overlap, and as a consequence critical gaps as well. If the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) is at the heart of the regional security architecture, then it needs to be very clear that the Pacific Islands Forum itself has both the mandate and oversight of these various different regional security institutions or arrangements, and so on.

The review of the regional architecture is seeking of clarify and streamline and better align the existing, already crowded and increasingly contested architecture, and these additional security arrangements overlay the existing murkiness that we do see in the region.

So it becomes very congested, but it also becomes congested in a number of critical ways, which is who decides on the rules for the region. For example, who makes the rules, who is the trusted partner, who is the trusted security partner, who upholds the rules, and who provides oversight?

All of those types of questions we need greater clarity on, and this is certainly something that, again, where civil society have been asking these questions loudly and frequently. We need to be finding those answers before the regional security architecture is inadvertently weakened as a consequence of this effort to strengthen it.

JB: Do you think there is a risk of developments in this space nudging the Pacific towards militarisation in a way that Pacific Islanders say they they deeply oppose?

AP: There is certainly a risk. Firstly, these agreements are certainly security agreements such as the Pukpuk Treaty, Veitacini Treaty between Australia and Fiji, the recent agreement that New Zealand just signed with Papua New Guinea, also with Cook Islands as well, amongst others, Nakamal (Vanuatu), Falepili (Tuvalu), and so forth from Australia.

Ans New Zealand's perspective, these agreements form a broader effort, which is very much about strategic denial and very much about securing the region through these binding Pacific Island countries to Australia, to New Zealand, and to a shared sense of collective security, and importantly, a shared sense of a collective threat landscape as well.

Now, obviously, Pacific countries will differ in how they view that threat landscape, and this is where it starts to get really tricky with these agreements, because there are certain demands, potentially. If you look at, for example, the agreement between Papua New Guinea and the United States, which gives the United States access to six different sites in Papua New Guinea, these could potentially bind Pacific countries to the United States, to Australia, to New Zealand in the case of any type of conflict in, for example, the Taiwan Straits.

So there are inherent risks here. Of course, Pacific countries have agency when they sign these agreements, but we also know that there is a degree of asymmetry when when it comes to power relationships as well. So there is that danger, yes.

JB: In the current dynamic geopolitics, we have seen PNG's government announce that it will close Taiwan's representative office in Port Moresby. That seems like a big development, would you agree? And what does that mean - a clear concession to China?

AP: Without a doubt. If you consider the fact that whittling down Taiwan's allies in the Pacific has been a central objective of Chinese engagement in the Pacific for several decades since the cheque book diplomacy years of the 1980s, 1990s, and it has been very successful in doing so.

I mean, within one week, we saw both Solomon Islands and and Kiribati switching diplomatic recognition, followed by Nauru. And now, there are only three Pacific countries who remain allied to, or recognise, Taiwan. So this is a very geopolitical move by by Papua New Guinea as well, and doing so is sending a very strong signal to China.

In fact, that is actually reflected in the comments made by Papua New Guinea when they announced that decision that the Chinese ambassador was informed of the decision, so it does send a very strong signal. But it also needs to be understood in terms of Papua New Guinea hedging and balancing its relationships between China and and and with Australia as well. So, it is not simply a case of alignment by any stretch of imagination. It is more a a strategy of hedging and balancing core relationships.

JB: The Taiwanese Trade Office is a feature in numerous Pacific countries where they otherwise do not formally recognise Taiwan diplomatically.

AP: Yes, exactly. These tensions have arisen before, in Fiji for instance, not so long ago as well. I think what people are concerned about is certainly the manner in which this was conducted. It was quite undiplomatic, and Taiwan is a valued economic partner of Papua New Guinea.

Taiwan imports something like a third of Papua New Guinea's LNG (liquefied natural gas) - so by no means an insignificant economic partner. The way that this was conducted, it was really very unfortunate [and] sends a very strong message in the lead up to the PIF leaders' meeting in Palau.

World.title: David Tamihere faces two-month wait to find out if he will be retried
World.content:
David Tamihere will have to wait another two months to find out whether he will be retried over the 1989 murder of two Swedish backpackers in Coromandel.

Tamihere appeared at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday on the charges he was first convicted of in 1990 but which were quashed by the Supreme Court in March.

The Supreme Court said it was up to Crown prosecutors to decide whether to hold a trial again.

Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock told the High Court on Wednedsay the Crown needed more time to decide whether it would try Tamihere again for the murder of Urban Höglin and Heidi Paakkonen.

Tamihere's lawyer James Carruthers said with a trial potentially a year away, the defence team was in the dark about the case.

They were dealing with events that happened 37 years ago and did not know what evidence or witnesses the prosecution was relying on.

Justice Mathew Downs agreed to the extension requested by the prosecution but gave it a deadline.

It must make a decision by the end of September, and Tamihere will appear again in October.

Arriving at court, Tamihere, who is now in his 70s, said he was feeling good but did not know what to expect.

He has been out of jail since 2010 when he was released on parole.

Crown solicitor Alysha McClintock at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

When the convictions were quashed, he was freed but is still facing the two murder charges.

The background

Höglin, 23, and Paakkonen, 21, were last seen in Thames in 1989.

Their disappearance and the subsequent trial was one of the country's highest profile crimes.

Many aspects remain a mystery.

Höglin's body was found in 1991, after Tamihere had been convicted, but Paakkonen's body has never been found.

At the time the couple went missing, Tamihere had been living in the bush in the Coromandel for about three years, in hiding from police over a prior rape charge.

Much of the Crown's original case was circumstantial.

It included evidence that Tamihere had been seen driving around the Coromandel region in the couple's ute.

Tamihere admitted dumping or selling their possession but maintained he had never met them.

The Crown's case also relied on testimony from former inmate Robert Conchie Harris who said Tamihere told him he killed the Swedes. However Harris was convicted of perjury over evidence in 2017.

The appeals

Tamihere first appealed his convictions in 1992, after Höglin's body was found wearing a watch that a prosecution witness had initially said he had seen at Tamihere's house.

The body was also 70km away from where the Crown first suspected he had been killed.

That appeal was unsuccessful but the 2017 perjury conviction of Harris prompted a new round of appeals from Tamihere.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal declined to quash the convictions, saying despite the problems with some crown evidence, there was still enough to safely say Tamihere was guilty.

The Supreme Court released its decision in March that finally quashed the convictions.

David Tamihere at the High Court session on Wednesday. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

It said Harris's evidence meant the trial was fundamentally unfair, and that there had been a "radical recasting" of the crown case since the original trial.

That effectively meant the case had never truly been tested by a jury.

The court said it was possible a jury would still find Tamihere guilty, but that could only be decided in a retrial.

Timeline

April 1989 - Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen and Sven Urban Höglin are last seen in Thames. Tamihere was on the run from police and living rough in the bush after pleading guilty to raping a woman three years earlier.

May 1989 - David Tamihere is arrested over an earlier rape. That same day, the couple are reported missing.

December 1990 - Tamihere is convicted of murdering the couple and sentenced to life imprisonment.

1991 - Höglin's body is found near Whangamatā.

1992 - The Court of Appeal rejects Tamihere's appeal.

1994 - Tamihere is denied leave to appeal to the Privy Council.

1995 - Witness C - later revealed as Roberto Conchie Harris - swears an affidavit retracting his evidence.

1996 - Harris retracts his retraction.

2010 - Tamihere is released on parole.

2016 - A private prosecution alleges Harris lied at Tamihere's trial.

2017 - Harris is sentenced after being found guilty of perjury and not guilty of perverting the course of justice.

2017 - Harris appeals the perjury convictions and sentence and fights to keep his identity hidden.

2018 - Harris drops his appeal against the perjury convictions.

2018 - The High Court revokes suppression order for Witness B, another prison informant.

2020 - Justice Minister Andrew Little announces Tamihere's case is going back to the Court of Appeal after a Royal Prerogative of Mercy is granted.

November 2023 - The Court of Appeal hears Tamihere's case.

July 2024 - The Court of Appeal declines to quash Tamihere's convictions.

December 2024 - The Supreme Court grants leave for the case to be heard there.

August 2025 - The case heads to the Supreme Court sitting in Auckland.
